nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\sigma'} \ar[r]^\phi& \{0,1, \dots, n\}\ar[d]^\sigma \\ I'\ar[r]_u& I, }
nodes.label: eq:comm-diagr-emb

nodes.name: Diagram identifying phi_2 = g^* phi_1
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)} \ar[r]^{\phi_2}& \{0,1,\dots, n\} \ar[d]^{\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma^2} \\ \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& \{0,1,\dots, n\}, }
nodes.label: eq:2.1.11

nodes.name: Direct construction of the restricted torsor
nodes.statement: Given a structure torsor \[ \mathcal{O}(I)\buildrel \rho\over\longrightarrow\operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}(\{0,1,\dots, n\}, I) \] for $I$, we can directly construct the ``restricted torsor" $\mathcal{O}(I')$ for $\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ and the canonical morphism \[ \psi=(\psi_*=u, \psi^*): (I', \mathcal{O}(I'))\to (I, \mathcal{O}(I)) \] as follows. Choose some $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$, so that $\sigma=\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}(f)$ is a bijection defining a total order on $I$. Let $\phi: [n']\to[n]$ be the monotone map in \eqref{eq:comm-diagr-emb}. To emphasize the dependence of $\phi$ on $f$, we denote it as $\phi=f^*\psi$ (where $\psi$ stands for the morphism we are constructing). For $g,h\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ put $f.g\sim f.h$ whenever $(f^*u)^*(g)=(f^*u)^*(h)$ in $\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$. It is immediate that this is an equivalence relation, independent on the choice of $f$. We put $\mathcal{O}(I')=\mathcal{O}(I)/\sim$ and define $\psi^*: {\mathcal O}(I) \to {\mathcal O}(I')$ to be the quotient map. The composite \[ {\mathcal O}(I) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}(\{0,1,\dots, n\}, I) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_ {{\bf FSet}}(\{0,1,\dots, n'\}, I) \] factors through $\psi^*$ providing a map $\rho_{I'}: {\mathcal O}(I') \to \operatorname{Isom}(\{0,1,\dots, n'\}, I)$. There exists a unique $\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$-action on ${\mathcal O}(I')$ such that, for every $f \in {\mathcal O}(I)$ and $g \in \mathfrak{G}_n$, we have \[ \psi^*(f.g) = \psi^*(f).((f^*\psi)^*g). \] It is now readily verified that this $\mathfrak{G}_m$-action on ${\mathcal O}(I)$ is simply transitive, and the maps $\psi_*=u$ and $\psi^*$ satisfy the conditions (i) and (ii) of Proposition \ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}.

nodes.name: Circle
nodes.statement: By a {\em circle} we mean a topological space homeomorphic to the standard circle $S^1$.

nodes.name: Marked circle
nodes.statement: By a {\em marked circle} we mean a pair $(C,J)$ where $C$ is a circle and $J\subset C$ is a nonempty closed subset homeomorphic to a finite disjoint union of copies of the interval $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Homeomorphisms of marked circles
nodes.statement: For two marked circles $(C,J)$ and $(C',J')$, we denote \[ { \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J')) \,\,=\,\,\bigl\{ \phi\in{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(C,C') \bigl| \,\, \phi(J)\subset J' \bigr\}. \]

nodes.name: Contractibility of components of marked-circle homeomorphisms
nodes.statement: Each connected component of ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J'))$ is contractible.
nodes.label: prop:homeo-contr

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.11
nodes.statement: Follows from the fact that the group of orientation preserving self-homeomorphisms of an interval is contractible.
nodes.statement_short: Orientation preserving self-homeomorphisms of an interval form a contractible group.

nodes.name: G-structured circle
nodes.statement: By a $G$-{\em structured circle}\footnote{A more precise term would be ``${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structured circle".} we mean a pair $(C,\rho)$ where $C$ is a circle, and $\rho: F\to{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ is a reduction of the structure group along $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$.

nodes.name: Structured homeomorphisms of G-structured circles
nodes.statement: For $G$-structured circles $(C,\rho)$ and $(C',\rho')$, we define ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G((C,\rho), (C',\rho'))$ to be the set of pairs $(\phi, \widetilde\phi)$, where $\phi\in{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(C,C')$ and $\widetilde\phi: F\to F'$ is a ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-equivariant homeomorphism such that the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ F\ar[d]_\rho \ar[r]^{\widetilde\phi}& F'\ar[d]^{\rho'} \\ { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C) \ar[r]_\phi & { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C') } \] is commutative.

nodes.name: Structured homeomorphisms of structured marked circles
nodes.statement: For $G$-structured marked circles $(C, J)$ and $(C',J')$, we denote by ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G((C,J), (C',J '))$ the closed subspace in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(C,C')$ formed by $(\phi,\widetilde\phi)$ such that $\phi\in { \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J '))$.

nodes.name: Category C_G of G-structured marked circles
nodes.statement: We define the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ with objects given by $G$-structured marked circles and morphisms \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{{ {\EuScript C}_G}}((C,J), (C',J')) = \pi_0\, { \operatorname{Homeo}}^G((C,J), (C',J ')). \]

nodes.name: Topological model of a planar crossed simplicial group
nodes.statement: Let $p: G \to O(2)$ be a planar Lie group with corresponding crossed simplicial group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$. Then the functor \[ \lambda_{{ {\EuScript C}_G}}: { {\EuScript C}_G} \longrightarrow {\bf FSet}, \quad (C,J)\mapsto \pi_0(J) \] canonically factors as in \[ \xymatrix{ { {\EuScript C}_G} \ar[dr]_{\lambda_{{ {\EuScript C}_G}}} \ar[rr]^{\pi}_{\simeq} & & {\mathcal G} \ar[dl]^{\lambda_{{\mathcal G}}} \\ & {\bf FSet} & } \] where ${\mathcal G}$ denotes the category of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets and $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\mathcal G}$ is an equivalence of categories. In particular, the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ is equivalent to ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Taking components of the marked subset gives an equivalence from structured marked circles $\mathcal{C}_G$ to structured sets $\mathcal{G}$, so $\mathcal{C}_G\simeq\Delta\mathfrak{G}$.
assumptions: Let $p: G \to O(2)$ be a planar Lie group with corresponding crossed simplicial group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
conclusions: ${\mathcal G}$ denotes the category of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets and $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\mathcal G}$ is an equivalence of categories.
In particular, the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ is equivalent to ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
nodes.label: thm:CG=DG

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.13
nodes.statement: Let $(C,J)$ be a marked $G$-structured circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure group along $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. We claim that the association \[ (C,J) \mapsto (\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)}), \] where $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ denotes the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set constructed in Lemma \ref{lem:pi0} below, extends to an equivalence of categories $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$. Given a morphism $(\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi}): (C,J) \to (C', J')$ of marked $G$-structured circles, we have to construct a morphism of the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ and $(\pi_0(J'),\rho_{\pi_0(J')})$. Clearly, we have an induced map $\psi: \pi_0(J) \to \pi_0(J')$ of underlying sets. We now define the pullback map $\psi^*: \pi_0(F_{J'}) \to \pi_0(F_{J})$ of structured frames. Let $f \in F_{J'}$ represent a structured frame in $\pi_0(F_{J'})$. Its image under $\rho$ defines a homeomorphism $\rho(f): { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C')$ which maps $[n]$ to $J'$. We choose a point in the unique component of $C'\setminus J'$ bounded by $\rho(f)(n)$ and $\rho(f)(0)$, and denote its preimage in $C$ under $\varphi$ by $p$. Note that $p$ lies in $C \setminus J$. Consider the homeomorphism $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$ in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$. Now we choose a path $\alpha: [0,1] \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ starting at $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$, ending at a homeomorphism which maps $[m]$ to $J$, such that, for all $t \in [0,1]$, $\alpha(t)(0) \ne p$. It is easy to see that the space of such paths is contractible. Since $F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ is a covering, there is a unique lift of $\alpha$ to $F$ satisfying $\alpha(0) = \widetilde{\varphi}$. We define $\psi^*(f)$ to be the connected component of $\alpha(1)$ in the space $F_J$. The pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ defines a morphism in $\mathcal{G}$ by Proposition \ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}. It straightforward to show that this construction is functorial. To see that it provides an equivalence of categories it suffices to verify the unique factorization property for the full subcategory of ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ generated by a set of standard objects $\{ (S^1, [n]) \}$ which is easily done.
nodes.statement_short: Construct pullback of frames via path lifting in the covering of homeomorphisms. Equivalence then reduces to unique factorization on standard objects.

nodes.name: Structured sets from structured marked circles
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 0$ and consider the standard circle $S^1$ equipped with the standard subset $[n] \subset S^1$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity. \begin{enumerate} \item Consider the subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \subset { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1)$ of homeomorphisms preserving which preserve the standard subset $[n]$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity. Let $H_n$ be the pullback \[ \xymatrix{ H_n\ar[d] \ar[r]&{ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1) \ar[d]^{p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}} \\ { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \ar[r]&{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1). } \] Then each connected component of $H_n$ is contractible and there is a canonical group isomorphism $\pi_0(H_n) \cong \mathfrak{G}_0$. \item Let $(C,J)$ be a $G$-structured marked circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure group along $ p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. Consider the subset ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J)) \subset { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ consisting of homeomorphisms which map $[n]$ into $J$ and let $\rho_J: F_J \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J))$ denote the restriction of $\rho$. Then the set $\pi_0(F_J)$ is a $\pi_0(H_n)$-torsor, equipped with a natural equivariant map \[ \rho_{\pi_0(J)}: \pi_0(F_J) \to \pi_0(J) \] making $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Components of the pullback $H_n$ are contractible with $\pi_0(H_n)\cong\mathfrak{G}_n$, and $\pi_0(J)$ of a structured marked circle is a $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structured set.
nodes.label: lem:pi0

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.14
nodes.statement: (1) As argued in Proposition \ref{prop:homeo-contr}, each component of the subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n])$ is contractible. Therefore, the map $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$ restricts to a covering $H_n \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1,[n])$ which is topologically trivial so that each connected component of $H_n$ must be contracible. We have \[ \pi_0 { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \cong D_{n+1} \cong \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_\Xi([n]) \] where $\Xi$ denotes the dihedral category of Example \ref {ex:dihedral}. The group $\pi_0(H_n)$ can be identified with the preimage $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})$ under $p: G\to O(2)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:crossed-groups}(b2), this preimage is canonically identified with $\mathfrak{G}_n$. \noindent (2) Passing to connected components, we obtain a sequence of maps \[ \pi_0(F_J) \overset{\pi_0(\rho_J)}{\longrightarrow} \pi_0({ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J))) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}([n], \pi_0(J)) \] whose composite is defined to be $\rho_{\pi_0(J)}$. It is apparent that $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set.
nodes.statement_short: Contractibility via the trivial covering over $\operatorname{Homeo}(S^1,[n])$ and identification with $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})$ using Theorem 1.33(b2).

nodes.name: Structured orders on finite subsets of structured circles
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $G$-structured circle. Then, for any nonempty finite subset $I\subset C$, both $I$ and $\pi_0(C-I)$ acquire canonical ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structures. These structures are natural with respect to homeomorphisms of $G$-structured circles.
conclusions: for any nonempty finite subset $I\subset C$, both $I$ and $\pi_0(C-I)$ acquire canonical ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structures.
These structures are natural with respect to homeomorphisms of $G$-structured circles.
nodes.label: cor:structured-circle-orders

nodes.name: Action of Homeo^G(S^1) on geometric realization (generalized Drinfeld)
nodes.statement: Let $R:{\mathcal Set}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}\to{\mathcal Top}$ be the geometric realization functor: $R(X)=|i^*X|$, where $i: \Delta\to{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is the embedding. The group ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$ acts on $R$ by natural isomoprhisms. In particular, it acts on each $|i^*X|$ be homeomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: The planar homeomorphism group acts by natural isomorphisms on the geometric realization of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-sets.

nodes.name: Homeo^G(S^1) is the automorphism group of geometric realization
nodes.statement: It seems plausible that the group ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$ is in fact identified with $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(R)$ which would provide its natural construction in terms of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.16
nodes.statement: The argument is similar to that of \cite{drinfeld:cyclic}. That is, let $\bf\Delta$ be the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, and ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta}\to \mathcal{G}$ be the functor of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure, extending $i$ (Example \ref{ex:DG-closure}). A simplicial set $Y$ can be seen as a contravariant functor $Y: {\bf\Delta}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and, as pointed out in Formula (1.1) of \cite {drinfeld:cyclic}, \[ |Y|\,\,=\,\,\varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, Y\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr), \] where $F$ runs over finite subsets of $[0,1]$, and $\pi_0([0,1]-F)$ is equipped by the total order induced by that on $[0,1]$. Now, if $X$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set, we can view $X$ as a contravariant functor $\mathcal{G}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and identify \[ \begin{gathered} |i^*X| \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, ({\bf i}^*X)\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr) \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0([0,1]-F))\bigr) \,\,= \\ =\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{1\in F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr) \,\,=\,\, \,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr). \end{gathered} \] Here we view $S^1$ as obtained from $[0,1]$ by identifying $0$ and $1$ into one point $1\in S^1$ and as equipped with the standard ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure. Each set $\pi_0(S^1-F)$ is then equipped with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure by Corollary \ref{cor:structured-circle-orders}. Now, the last colimit is manifestly acted upon by ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Following Drinfeld, write the realization as a colimit over finite subsets of the circle; the colimit is manifestly acted on by $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$.

nodes.name: Self-duality of planar crossed simplicial groups
nodes.statement: Any planar crossed simplicial group is self-dual.
nodes.statement_short: Every planar crossed simplicial group is self-dual.
nodes.label: cor:duality

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.17
nodes.statement: We define the functor $(-)^{\vee}: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to { {\EuScript C}_G}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ by putting \[ (C,J)^{\vee} := (C, \overline{C \setminus J}), \quad (\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi})^{\vee} := (\varphi^{-1}, \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1}) \] on objects and morphisms, respectively. Since the square of this functor equals the identity functor, it must be an equivalence. Further, since ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is equivalent to ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$, we conclude that there exists a duality functor $(-)^\vee_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \overset{\simeq}{\to} {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\operatorname{op}}$ with $[n]^\vee=[n]$. The choice of values for this functor on morphisms, however, is not canonical.
nodes.statement_short: Complement-of-marking duality on $\mathcal{C}_G$ is an involution, transported via $\mathcal{C}_G\simeq\Delta\mathfrak{G}$.

nodes.name: Interstices
nodes.statement: The connected components of $\overline{C \setminus J}$ can be regarded as ``interstices" positioned between adjacent connected components of $J$.

nodes.name: Linear growth of G_n from duality
nodes.statement: After choosing a duality functor $(-)^\vee_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$, we obtain identifications of sets \[ \begin{gathered} \mathfrak{G}_n \,\, \buildrel \operatorname{C.F.} \over = \,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([n], [0]) \,\,\simeq \,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0]^\vee, [n]^\vee)\,\,\simeq \\ \simeq \,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n]) \,\, \buildrel \operatorname{C.F.} \over = \,\, \mathfrak{G}_0 \times \operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n]), \end{gathered} \] where ``C.F." stands for the canonical factorization of morphisms in a crossed simplicial group. These identifications can be interpreted by saying that $\mathfrak{G}_n$ ``grows linearly with $n$" (with ``coefficient of proportionality" being $\mathfrak{G}_0$). Cf. the discussion of three growth types of crossed simplicial groups in \S \ref{sub:weyl}. We further deduce that the $\mathfrak{G}_n$-action on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n])$ is simply transitive.
nodes.label: rems:duality

nodes.name: Combinatorial duality of structured sets
nodes.statement: One can also give a purely combinatorial description of duality in terms of the category $\mathcal{G}$ of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets. Note that for any object $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))\in{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ we have canonical identifications \[ I \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{G}([0], I)/\mathfrak{G}_0, \quad \mathcal{O}(I) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{G}(I, [0]). \] The dual of $(I, {\mathcal O}(I))$ is the pair \[ (I^{\vee}, {\mathcal O}(I^{\vee})) := (\operatorname{Hom}_{{\mathcal G}}(I, [0])/\mathfrak{G}_0, \operatorname{Hom}_{{\mathcal G}}([0],I)) \] which can be made into a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set so that $I \mapsto I^{\vee}$ defines an equivalence ${\mathcal G} \to {\mathcal G}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$.

nodes.name: Total cyclic order on a finite set
nodes.statement: A {\em (total) cyclic order} on a finite set $J$ of cardinality $n$ is the choice of a simply transitive action of the group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Note that a cyclic order on the set $J$ is uniquely determined by specifying for every element $j$ its {\em successor} $j + 1$.
nodes.genus: choice of a simply transitive action of the group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.label: def:totalcyclic

nodes.name: Examples of cyclic orders
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Any set of cardinality $\le 2$ has a unique cyclic order. A cyclic order on a set $J$ of cardinality $3$ is the same as an orientation of the triangle $|\Delta^J|$. \item Every subset of a cyclically ordered set $J$ has a canonical cyclic order. \item Any finite linearly ordered set $J$ carries a canonical cyclic order where the successor of each nonmaximal element of $J$ is its successor with respect to the linear order and the minimal element is the successor of the maximal element. We say that this cyclic order is the {\em cyclic closure} of the linear order on $J$. \item More generally, given a cyclically ordered finite set $K$ and a map of finite sets $f: J \to K$ where each fiber of $f$ is equipped with a linear order, we can define the {\em lexicographic} cyclic order on $J$ as follows. First note, that the set of fibers of $f$ is canonically identified with $K$ and hence carries a cyclic order. Therefore, every fiber has a successor fiber. Now the cyclic order on $J$ is given as follows: For every element $j$ which is nonmaximal in its fiber, we define the successor $j +1$ to be the successor with respect to the specified linear order of the fiber. If $j$ is maximal in its fiber, we define its successor to be the minimal element of the successor fiber. Here the convention is to skip all empty fibers. The previous example is then given by the case when $K$ is a point, equipped with its unique cyclic order. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Cyclic closure of a linear order
nodes.statement: We say that this cyclic order is the {\em cyclic closure} of the linear order on $J$.

nodes.name: Morphisms of cyclically ordered sets and large cyclic category
nodes.statement: A morphism $f: J \to K$ of finite cyclically ordered sets is a map $f: J \to K$ of underlying sets equipped with the choice of a linear order on every fiber such that the cyclic order on $J$ is the induced lexicographic order. The resulting category ${\bf \Lambda}$ given by finite nonempty cyclically ordered sets and their morphisms is called the {\em large cyclic category.}

nodes.name: Large cyclic category contains Connes' category and large simplex category
nodes.statement: (a) Restricting to the standard cyclic ordinals $\langle n \rangle$, this gives a purely combinatorial description of morphisms in Connes' category $\Lambda$. (b) We have a natural faithful embedding ${\bf \Delta} \subset {\bf \Lambda}$ given by associating to a linearly ordered set $J$ its cyclic closure. This extends the embedding $\Delta\subset\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Partial cyclic order
nodes.statement_short: Ternary relation satisfying reflexivity, antisymmetry, transitivity, cyclic symmetry and a 2-cycle axiom; total if comparability holds.
nodes.label: def:cyclic-order

nodes.name: Examples of partial cyclic orders
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Let $C$ be a circle. Then $C^3_\neq = C^3-\bigcup_{i\neq j} \{x_i=x_j\}$ has two connected components which are in bijection with orientations of $C$. The ``anti-clockwise" component corrresponding to a choice of orientation contains triples $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ with $x_i$ following very closely each other in the orientation direction. The closure $\lambda$ of this component is a total cyclic order on $C$. In particular, the standard oriented circle $S^1 = \{|z|=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}$ has a canonical cyclic order. This implies that a total cyclic order on a finite set $J$ can be defined as an homeomorphism class of embeddings of $J$ into oriented circles. That is, two such embeddings $u: J\to C$ and $u':J\to C'$ are identified iff there is an orientation preserving homeomorphism $\phi: C\to C'$ such that $\phi u=u'$. It is now easy to verify that a total cyclic order on a finite set as defined in Definition \ref{def:cyclic-order} is the same as a total cyclic order in the sense of Definition \ref{def:totalcyclic}. \item Let $\leq$ be a partial linear order on $S$. Its {\em cyclic closure} is the ternary relation $\lambda=\lambda_\leq\subset S^3$ obtained as the closure of the set $\{x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3\}$ under the action of $\mathbb{Z}/3$ by cyclic rotations. It is straightforward to see that $\lambda$ is a partial cyclic order, total if $\leq$ is a total linear order, cf. \cite[Th. 3.5]{novak}. This implies that total cyclic order on a finite set $J$ with $|J|=n$ is the same as a class of bijections $J\to \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ under the action of $\mathbb{Z}/n$, each bijection (i.e., a total order) giving a cyclic order by cyclic closure. \item Every set $J$ has the {\em discrete partial cyclic order} consisting only of triples $(a,a,a)$, $a\in J$. If $|J|=1$, this is the only partial cyclic order on $J$. If $|J|=2$, then $J$ has two partial cyclic orders: one discrete and the other is the total cyclic order, formed by all triples $(a,b,c)\in J^3$. Note that Nov\'ak's setting \cite{novak} allows only one partial cyclic order on a 2-element set, the discrete one. \item Generalizing (1), one can see that the set of points of any ``abstract circle" in the sense of Moerdijk \cite{moerdijk} has a total cyclic order. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: ex:cyclic-orders

nodes.name: Partial cyclic order on flag varieties (Fock-Goncharov)
nodes.statement: The real projective line $\mathbb{R} P^1$, being a circle, has a cyclic order. Such an order is determined by a choice of orientation of $\mathbb{R}^2$. More generally, let $F_n=\operatorname{Flag}(1,2,...,n; \mathbb{R}^n)$ be the space of complete flags in $\mathbb{R}^n$. For example, $F_2=\mathbb{R} P^1$. One of the main results of \cite{fock-goncharov} (theory of positive configurations of flags) says, in our terminology, that $F_n$ has a natural partial cyclic order $\lambda$, determined by a choice of orientation of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Explicitly, a closed smooth curve $C\subset \mathbb{R} P^{n-1}$ is called {\em convex}, if every hyperplane intersects $C$ in at most $n-1$ points. In particular, such $C$ does not lie in a hyperplane. Taking the osculating flags to $C$ at all its points, we obtain an embedding $\gamma_C: C\to F_n$. The 2-element set of orientations of any convex curve $C\subset \mathbb{R} P^{n-1}$ is canonically identified with the 2-element set of orientations of $\mathbb{R}^n$, by a version of the Frenet frame construction (this is the old-fashioned definition of the orientation of the space in terms of ``left and right screws"). Thus choosing an orientation of $\mathbb{R}^n$, we equip any convex $C$ with a total cyclic order $\lambda_C$. We then say that $({\bf f}_1, {\bf f}_2, {\bf f}_3)\in F_n^3$ lies in $\lambda$, if there is a convex curve $C\in \mathbb{R} P^{n-1}$ and three points $(t_1, t_2, t_3)\in\lambda_C$ such that ${\bf f}_i=\gamma_C(t_i)$. See {\em loc. cit.} for more details as well as a generalization to the complete flag variety of any split simple algebraic group over $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Lexicographic cyclic order
nodes.statement:
Let $f: I	o J$ be a map of sets. Suppose that $J$ is equipped with a partial cyclic order $\lambda_J$, and each fiber $f^{-1}(j)$ is equipped with a partial linear order $\leq_j$. In this setting we construct a partial cyclic order $\lambda=\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))$ on $I$, called the {\em lexicographic cyclic order} as follows. We say that $(a,b,c)\in\lambda_I$ if $(f(a), f(b), f(c))\in\lambda_J$ and either  egin{enumerate}[labelindent=1cm] \item[(i)] all three elements $f(a), f(b), f(c)$ are distinct, or: \item[(ii)] $f(a)=f(b)
eq f(c)$ and $a\leq_{f(a)} b$, or: \item[(ii')] $f(a)=f(c)
eq f(b)$ and $c\leq_{f(c)} a$, or: \item[(ii'')] $f(a)
eq f(b)=f(c)$ and $b\leq_{f(b)} c$, or: \item[(iii)] $f(a)=f(b)=f(c)$ and either  egin{enumerate} \item $a\leq_j b\leq_j c$, or \item $b\leq_j c\leq_j a$, or \item $c\leq_j a\leq_j b$, \,\, $j=f(a)=f(b)=f(c)$. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate} If $\lambda_J$ is a total cyclic order, and each $\leq_i$ is a total linear order, then $\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))$ is a total cyclic order.
nodes.label: defi:lexico

nodes.name: Morphisms of partially cyclically ordered sets
nodes.statement: Let $(I,\lambda_I)$ and $(J, \lambda_J)$ be partially cyclically ordered sets. \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),itemsep=0cm,topsep=1ex] \item Assume that $\lambda_I$ is a total cyclic order. Then we define a {\em morphism} $F: I\to J$ to be a datum consisting of a map $f: I\to J$ and a total linear order $\leq_j$ on each $f^{-1}(j)$ such that $\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))=\lambda_I$. \item In general, a morphism $F: I\to J$ is a compatible system of morphisms $I'\to J$ given for all totally cyclically ordered subsets $I'\subset I$ (with respect to the induced cyclic order). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:morphisms-cyclic-orders

nodes.name: Category of partially cyclically ordered sets
nodes.statement: The collection of partially cyclically ordered sets with morphisms as defined above forms a category ${\mathbf \Lambda}_{\operatorname{par}}$ which contains the categories $\Lambda$ and ${\bf \Lambda}$ as full subcategories.

nodes.name: Cyclic dual and linear refinements
nodes.statement: Given a cyclically ordered set $J$ of cardinality $n \ge 1$, the set $J^{\vee} := \operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(J, \langle 0\rangle)$ is, by definition, in canonical bijection with the set of {\em linear refinements} of the cyclic order on $J$, i.e., linear orders whose cyclic closure recovers the cyclic order on $J$.

nodes.name: Interstices of a subset of the circle
nodes.statement: Let $J \subset S^1$ be a subset of the standard circle. Providing $J$ with the counter-clockwise cyclic order induced from $S^1$, we may identify the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(J, \langle 0\rangle)$ with the set of homotopy classes of monotone maps $f: S^1 \to S^1$ of degree $1$ taking the subset $J$ to $1 \in S^1$. Let us refer to the arcs on $S^1$ which connect an element of $J$ to its successor as {\em interstices of $J$}. The map $f$ is uniquely determined by specifying which interstice of $J$ maps to a nontrivial loop in $S^1$. Therefore, $J^{\vee}$ is canonically identified with the set of interstices of $J \subset S^1$. For an abstract cyclically ordered set, the set $J^{\vee}$ should be regarded as an intrinsic construction of the set of interstices with its cyclic order, without any reference to an embedding into the circle. The role of $J^\vee$ as a dual object was emphasized by Drinfeld \cite{drinfeld:cyclic} whose result can be formulated as follows.

nodes.name: Cyclic interstice duality (Drinfeld)
nodes.statement: The cyclic interstice construction $J \mapsto J^{\vee}$ extends to a functor \[ {\bf \Lambda}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\bf \Lambda} \] which is an equivalence of categories.
nodes.statement_short: $J\mapsto J^\vee$ is an anti-autoequivalence of the large cyclic category.
nodes.label: prop:cyclic-interstice

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.30
nodes.statement: Although this is a particular case of the general duality for planar crossed simplicial groups, let us provide a self-contained proof for convenience of the reader. Given a morphism of cyclically ordered sets $f: J \to K$, we obtain a map of sets of linear refinements $f^{\vee}: K^{\vee} \to J^{\vee}$. To lift this map to a morphism of cyclically ordered sets, we have to additionally provide a linear order on each fiber of $f^{\vee}$. Consider linear orders $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \in K^{\vee}$ which map to the same linear order $\lambda \in J^{\vee}$. Let $j_{\max}$ be the maximum of $(J, \lambda)$. We say $\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2$ if \[ \big|\{k \in K\; |\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_1} k\}\big| \le \big|\{k \in K \;|\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_2} k\}\big|. \] This construction provides linear orders on the fibers of $f^{\vee}$ which are compatible with the cyclic order on $K^{\vee}$. The equivalence of categories can be verified by noting that the double dual $(J^{\vee})^{\vee}$ can be canonically and functorially identified with $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Order the fibers of $f^\vee$ by comparing positions of $f(j_{\max})$; double dual returns $J$.

nodes.name: Opposite cyclic order
nodes.statement: Given a finite set $J$ with cyclic order $\lambda$, we can define the {\em opposite} cyclic order $\lambda^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ on $J$ by declaring the successor $j+1$ of an element $j$ to be the predecessor $j-1$ of $j$ with respect to $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Dihedral order on a finite set
nodes.statement: A {\em dihedral order} on a finite set $J$ of cardinality $\ge 3$ is defined to be the choice of a set $o(J) = \{\lambda_0,\lambda_1\}$ of opposite cyclic orders on $J$. A dihedral order on a set $J$ of cardinality $\le 2$ is defined to be the choice of an arbitrary two-element set $o(J)$. Given a dihedrally ordered set $(J, o(J))$, we refer to the two-element set $o(J)$ as the {\em orientation torsor} of $J$.
nodes.statement_short: A pair of opposite cyclic orders, or an arbitrary two-element orientation torsor for small sets.

nodes.name: Large dihedral category
nodes.statement: A morphism $J \to K$ of dihedrally ordered sets is defined to be a bijection $f: o(J) \to o(K)$ and an unordered pair $\{f_0:(J,\lambda_0) \to (K, f(\lambda_0)),f_1: (J, \lambda_1) \to (K, f(\lambda_1))\}$ of opposite morphisms of cyclic ordinals. Here, we agree by convention that for a dihedrally ordered set $J$ of cardinality $\le 2$, both elements of the orientation torsor $o(J)$ induce the unique cyclic order on $J$. With this notion of morphism, the set of finite nonempty dihedrally ordered sets organizes into a category ${\bf \Xi}$ which we call the {\em large dihedral category}.

nodes.name: Virtual orientation torsors and the quotient of the large cyclic category
nodes.statement: (a) The reason for the introduction of a ``virtual'' orientation torsor for sets of cardinality $\le 2$ should now be clear. For example, with this convention, the automorphism groups of the standard dihedrally ordered sets $\{0\}$ and $\{0,1\}$ are $D_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $D_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2$, respectively. The nontrivial automorphism given by interchanging the elements of the virtual orientation torsor acts trivially on the underlying sets. \vskip .2cm (b) The automorphism of $\bf \Lambda$ given by passing to the opposite cyclic order can be regarded as an action of the (discrete $2$-) group $\mathbb{Z}/2$ on $\bf \Lambda$. Our approach amounts to defining $\bf\Xi$ as the quotient of $\bf\Lambda$ by this action.

nodes.name: Examples of dihedral orders
nodes.label: exa:dihedral

nodes.name: Dihedral orders and real points of M_{0,J}
nodes.statement: A more algebro-geometric version of Example \ref{exa:dihedral} \ref{exa:item2} can be obtained as follows. Let $J$ be a finite set with $\geq 3$ elements, and $\overline M_{0,J}$ be the moduli space of stable $J$-pointed curves of genus 0. This is a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb{Q}$ of dimension $|J|-3$ whose open part is the quotient \[ M_{0,J} = \bigl( (\mathbb{P}^1)^J \setminus (\text{diagonals} )\bigr) \bigl/ PGL_2, \] see, e.g., \cite{kapranov-veronese} for more details. Now note that connected components of the real locus $M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ are in bijection with dihedral orders on $J$. Indeed, $\mathbb{R} P^1= \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{R})$ is topologically a circle, and action of $PGL_2(\mathbb{R})$ on it contains transformations both preserving and reversing the orientation of this circle, so a comparison as in Example \ref{exa:dihedral} \eqref{exa:item2} is immediate. It was proved in \cite{kapranov-permuto} that the closure in $\overline M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ of each component of $M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$, is identified with the Stasheff polytope $K_{|J|-1}$. Thus $\overline M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ can be obtained by gluing as many Stasheff polytopes as there are dihedral orders on $J$.

nodes.name: Distinct tuples and the 4-ary dihedral relation gamma
nodes.statement:
For any $n\geq 1$ let \[ J^n_
eq = J^n \setminus  igcup_{i
eq j} \{x_i=x_j\} \] be the set of $n$-tuples of distinct elements of $J$, and let $\gamma \subset J^4_
eq$ consist of $4$-tuples $(a,b,c,d)$ such that dihedral order on $\{a,b,c,d\}$ induced from the embedding into $J$ coincides with the dihedral closure of the linear order $(a,b,c,d)$.

nodes.name: Face operation removing the i-th element
nodes.statement: For any ${\bf x}= (x_0, \dots , x_4)\in J^5_\neq$ let \[ \partial_i {\bf x} = (x_0, \dots, \widehat x_i, \dots, x_4), \quad i=0, \dots, 4, \] be the tuple obtained by removing the $i$th element.

nodes.name: Pentagon property for dihedral orders
nodes.statement: Let $J$ be a finite dihedrally ordered set, $|J|\geq 5$, and $\gamma\subset J^4_\neq$ defined as above. For any ${\bf x}=(x_0, \dots, x_4) \in J^5_\neq$ the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] All $\partial_i {\bf x}$, $i=0, \dots, 4$, belong to $\gamma$. In order words, the total order on $\{x_0, \dots, x_4\}$ is compatible with the induced cyclic order. \item[(ii)] $\partial_1{\bf x}$ and $\partial_3 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$. \item[(iii)] $\partial_0{\bf x}$, $\partial_2{\bf x}$ and $\partial_4 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For five distinct elements, compatibility of all four-element faces with the dihedral order follows from faces 1,3 or faces 0,2,4.
assumptions: Let $J$ be a finite dihedrally ordered set, $|J|\geq 5$, and $\gamma\subset J^4_\neq$ defined as above.

nodes.name: Proof of the pentagon property
nodes.statement: Clearly, (i) implies (ii) and (iii). Let us prove that (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i). Let $J\hookrightarrow C$ be an embedding into a circle defining the dihedral order. Since $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$, we have that $x_0, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are in the right dihedral order. In other words, their embedding into a circle $C$ is such that they subdivide $C$ into the following (unoriented) arcs: $A(x_0, x_2)$, $A(x_2, x_3)$, $A(x_3, x_4)$ and $A(x_4, x_0)$. Here $A(x_p, x_q)$ denotes the arc joining $x_p, x_q$ which does not contain any other $x_j, j\in \{0,2,3,4\}$. With respect to this embedding into $C$, the point $x_1$ must lie on one of these arcs, and (i) holds precisely when $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$. Now, the assumption that $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ means that the diagonal $[x_0, x_2]$ crosses the diagonal $[x_1, x_4]$ which means that $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$. The proof that (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is similar. In fact, the conditions $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$ and $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ already imply (i), the situation differing from (ii) by a cyclic rotation.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $J$ in a circle and locate $x_1$ on an arc using diagonal crossings.

nodes.name: Dihedral dual
nodes.statement: Given any finite nonempty dihedrally ordered set $J$, consider the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}} := \operatorname{Hom}_{{\bf \Xi}}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$. We can identify the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}}$ with the set of pairs $(\lambda, o)$ where $o \in O(J)$ is an orientation and $\lambda$ is a linear refinement of the cyclic order on $J$ corresponding to $o$. In particular, $\widetilde{J^{\vee}}$ admits a natural involution given by $(\lambda,o) \mapsto (\lambda^{{\operatorname{op}}}, o^{{\operatorname{op}}})$. We define $J^{\vee}$ to be the orbit set under this involution. We can interpret $O(J)$ as an orientation torsor for $J^{\vee}$ which determines opposite cyclic orders on $J^{\vee}$. Hence $J^{\vee}$ admits a canonical dihedral order.

nodes.name: Oriented and unoriented interstices
nodes.statement: Let $J \subset S^1$ be a subset of the standard circle considered without chosen orientation. Then $J$ inherits a natural dihedral order and the morphism set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$ can be identified with homotopy classes of monotone homotopy equivalences $f:S^1 \to S^1$ which map the subset $J$ to the point $1 \in S^1$ where we orient the target circle counterclockwise. This map $f$ is uniquely determined by the choice of an orientation and the choice of an interstice which maps to a nontrivial loop in $S^1$. Therefore, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$ is in natural bijection with the set of {\em oriented interstices} of $J \subset S^1$. The quotient set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})/(\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is then identified with the set of {\em unoriented interstices}. The two possible choice of coherent orientations of all interstices correspond to the elements of the orientation torsor.

nodes.name: Dihedral interstice duality
nodes.statement: The dihedral interstice construction $J \mapsto J^{\vee}$ extends to a functor \[ {\bf \Xi}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\bf \Xi} \] which is an equivalence of categories. \qed
nodes.statement_short: $J\mapsto J^\vee$ is an anti-autoequivalence of the large dihedral category.
nodes.label: prop:dihedral-interstice

nodes.name: Paracyclic order on a finite set
nodes.statement: A {\em paracyclic order} on a finite nonempty set $J$ consists of \begin{enumerate} \item a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor $\widetilde{J}$, \item a surjection $\pi: \widetilde{J} \to J$ which exhibits $J$ as the orbit set of the bijection \[T:\; \widetilde{J} \to \widetilde{J},\quad \widetilde{j} \mapsto \widetilde{j} + |J|.\] \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Paracyclic orders from a base point on an oriented circle
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be an oriented circle. A choice of a base point $c\in C$ defines a canonical paracyclic order on any finite nonempty $J\subset C$. More precisely, the choice of $c$ produces a canonical universal covering $\pi: \widetilde C_c\to C$, with $\widetilde C_c$ being homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ and oriented, and so equipped with a canonical total order. The discrete subset $\widetilde j=\pi^{-1}(J)$ has a natural successor operation induced by the order on $\widetilde C_c$, which makes it into a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor. The generator of the group $\mathbb{Z}$ of deck transformations on $\widetilde C_c$ corresponds to the shift by $|J|$ in this torsor structure.
nodes.label: exa:paracyclic-exp

nodes.name: Large paracyclic category
nodes.statement: A morphism $(J, \widetilde{J}) \to (K, \widetilde{K})$ of paracyclically ordered sets is given by a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widetilde{J} \ar[d]_{\pi_J} \ar[r]^{\widetilde{f}} & \ar[d]^{\pi_K} \widetilde{K}\\ J \ar[r]^f & K } \] such that $\widetilde{f}$ is monotone with respect to the linear orders on $\widetilde{J}$ and $\widetilde{K}$ induced from the $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor structures. The resulting category of finite nonempty paracyclically ordered sets is called the {\em large paracyclic category} denoted by ${\bf \Lambda_{\infty}}$.

nodes.name: Z-ordered set
nodes.statement: Following \cite[\S 3.1]{HSS1}, call a $\mathbb{Z}$-{\em ordered set} as pair $(S,F)$, consisting of a partially ordered set $(S,\leq)$ and an morphism of partially ordered set $F: S\to S$.

nodes.name: Partial paracyclic order
nodes.statement: A {\em partial paracyclic order} on a set $J$ is a datum of: \begin{enumerate} \item a $\mathbb{Z}$-ordered set $(\widetilde J, F)$ such that $F$ is a fixed point-free bijection. We denote by $F^\mathbb{Z}$ the group of automorphisms of $S$ generated by $F$. \item A bijection $\widetilde J/F^\mathbb{Z}\to J$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Paracyclic order on lattices (Bruhat-Tits)
nodes.statement: (Cf. \cite{HSS1}, Ex. 3.1.5) Let $\mathbf{k}$ be a discrete valued field with the ring of integers $\mathfrak o$ and uniformizing element $\varpi$. Then the set $B=GL(n, \mathbf{k})/GL(n, \mathfrak{o})$ is identified with the set of $\mathfrak o$-lattices $L\subset \mathbf{k}^n$, so it is partially ordered by inclusion of lattices. The automorphism $F$ given by multiplication of (matrices or lattices) by the scalar matrix $\varpi$, makes $B$ into a $\mathbb{Z}$-ordered set. The quotient \[ B/\varpi^\mathbb{Z} \,\,=\,\, PGL(n, \mathbf{k})/PGL(n, \mathfrak{o}) \] has therefore a canonical (partial) paracyclic order.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyckerhoff-Kapranov, Higher Segal spaces I, Ex. 3.1.5

nodes.name: Point with trivial paracyclic order
nodes.statement: We denote by $\operatorname{pt}\nolimits$ the set $\{0\}$ equipped with the paracyclic order given by the trivial $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor.

nodes.name: Paracyclic dual
nodes.statement: Given a finite nonempty paracyclically ordered set $(J, \widetilde{J})$, consider the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}} := \operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Lambda_{\infty}}(J, \operatorname{pt}\nolimits)$ and define $J^{\vee}$ to be the orbit set under the translation action of $\mathbb{Z}$ on $\operatorname{pt}\nolimits$.

nodes.name: Paracyclic interstices
nodes.statement: Let $J \subset S^1$ and consider the paracyclic order $\pi^{-1}(J) \to J$ on $J$ induced from the universal cover map $\pi: \mathbb{R} \to S^1$ (corresponding to the base point $1\in S^1$. Then we can identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Lambda_{\infty}}(J, \operatorname{pt}\nolimits)$ with homotopy classes of monotone maps $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ which \begin{enumerate} \item map the subset $\widetilde{J} \subset \mathbb{R}$ to the subset $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$, \item are equivariant with respect to translation by $|J|$ on $\widetilde{J}$ and translation by $1$ on $\mathbb{Z}$. \end{enumerate} Any such homotopy class is uniquely determined by specifying the interstice $[\widetilde{j},\widetilde{j}+1]$ of $\widetilde{J} \subset \mathbb{R}$ which maps onto the interstice $[0,1]$ of $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$. Thus the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}}$ can be naturally identified with the set of interstices of $\widetilde{J} \subset \mathbb{R}$. The quotient $J^{\vee}$ can therefore be canonically identified with the set of interstices of $J \subset S^1$.

nodes.name: Paracyclic interstice duality
nodes.statement: The interstice construction $J \mapsto J^{\vee}$ extends to a functor \[ ({\bf \Lambda_{\infty}})^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\bf \Lambda_{\infty}} \] which is an equivalence of categories. \qed

nodes.name: Kernel K of a planar Lie group
nodes.statement: We denote $K=\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits(p)=\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits(\mathbbm{p})$.

nodes.name: Preserving orientation
nodes.statement: We say that $\mathbb{G}$ {\em preserves orientation} if $\mathbbm{p}(\mathbb{G})\subset GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$.

nodes.name: Kernel exact sequences for G
nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} 0\to K\longrightarrow \mathbb{G} \longrightarrow GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})\to 1, \\ 0\to K\longrightarrow \mathbb{G} \longrightarrow GL(2,\mathbb{R})\to 1. \end{gathered}
nodes.label: eq:group-K

nodes.name: Kernel K of a planar Lie group
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be the crossed simplicial group corresponding to $\mathbb{G}$. Then $K=\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits\{\rho: \mathfrak{G}_0\to \mathbb{Z}/2\}$. \item[(b)] The kernels corresponding to the various planar groups are given by:\\ \begin{tabular}{ p{1cm} || p{2cm}| p{2cm}| p{2cm}|p{2cm}|p{2cm}} $G$& $\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$& $\widetilde{SO(2)}$ & $\operatorname{Pin}^+_N(2)$ & $\widetilde {O(2)}$& $\operatorname{Pin}^-_{2M}(2)$ \\ \hline $K$ & $\mathbb{Z}/N$ & $\mathbb{Z}$ & $\mathbb{Z}/N$ & $\mathbb{Z}$ & $\mathbb{Z}/2M$ \end{tabular}\\ If $G$ does not preserve orientation then $\tau$ acts on $K$ by $\tau(k)=-k$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $K$ is the kernel of the parity of $\mathfrak{G}_0$, explicitly $\mathbb{Z}/N$, $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}/2M$, with $\tau$ acting by $-1$ in the nonorientable case.
nodes.label: prop:group-K

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: Follows from Proposition \ref{prop:orient-G-0} (a) and (b) respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Read off from Proposition 1.34.

nodes.name: Surface
nodes.statement: By a {\em surface} we will mean a connected $C^\infty$-surface $S$ possibly with boundary $\partial S$.

nodes.name: Frame bundle Fr_S
nodes.statement: Given a surface $S$, let $\operatorname{Fr}_S\to S$ be the principal $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$-bundle of frames in the tangent bundle $T_S$.

nodes.name: Orientation torsor of a surface
nodes.statement: The sheaf of connected components $\underline{\pi}_0(\operatorname{Fr}_S)$ is a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-torsor over $S$ which we call the {\em orientation torsor} of $S$ and denote by ${\operatorname{or}}_S$.

nodes.name: Twisted local system K^or
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathbb{G}$ does not preserve orientation. In this case, the $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$-action on $K$ from \eqref {eq:group-K} together with the $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$-torsor $\operatorname{Fr}_S\to S$, gives rise to a local system of abelian groups $\underline K^{\operatorname{or}}$ on $S$, locally isomorphic to $\underline{K}$.

nodes.name: G-structured surface
nodes.statement: A $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface is a datum $(S,F)$, where $S$ is a surface, and $F\buildrel\rho\over\to \operatorname{Fr}_S$ is a reduction of structure groups along $\mathbbm{p}$.
differentia: $F\buildrel\rho\over\to \operatorname{Fr}_S$ is a reduction of structure groups along $\mathbbm{p}$

nodes.name: Examples of G-structured surfaces
nodes.statement: We give examples using the notation of Table \ref{table:corr}. \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})] \item For $G=O(2)$, we have $\mathbb{G}=GL(2,\mathbb{R})$, and a $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface is just a surface with no additional structure. \item For $G=SO(2)$, we have $\mathbb{G}=GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$, and a $\mathbb{G}$-structure on $S$ is the same as an orientation of $S$. \item For $G=\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$, the group $\mathbb{G}$ is the $N$-fold connected covering of $GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$, and a $\mathbb{G}$-structure is known as an $N$-{\em spin structure}. The case $N=2$, being an instance of the spinor construction existing in any number of dimensions, has been studied more systematically, cf. \cite{johnson}. \item For the unversal covering $G=\widetilde{SO(2)}$ of $SO(2)$, the group $\mathbb{G}=\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$ is the universal covering of $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$. A $\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$-structure on a surface will be called a {\em framing}. Note that, in our definition, a framing on $S$ is a discrete datum: not an actual choice of a trivialization of $T_S$ but what amounts to an isotopy class of such trivializations. In fact, the same is true in all the other cases, and this is the reason for working with $\mathbb{G}$ instead of $G$. For instance, an $O(2)$-structure on $S$ is a Riemannian metric, while a $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$-structure is no extra structure at all. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: N-spin structure
nodes.statement: For $G=\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$, the group $\mathbb{G}$ is the $N$-fold connected covering of $GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$, and a $\mathbb{G}$-structure is known as an $N$-{\em spin structure}.

nodes.name: Framing of a surface
nodes.statement: A $\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$-structure on a surface will be called a {\em framing}.

nodes.name: Structured diffeomorphism of G-structured surfaces
nodes.statement: A {\em structured diffeomorphism} of $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces $(S,F)\to (S', F')$ is a pair $(\phi,\widetilde \phi)$ where $\phi: S\to S'$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\widetilde\phi: F\to F'$ is a $\mathbb{G}$-equivariant diffeomorphism lifting $d\phi: \operatorname{Fr}_S\to\operatorname{Fr}_{S'}$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism of G-structures
nodes.statement: A structured diffeomorphism $(S,F) \to (S,F')$ with $\phi=\operatorname{Id}\nolimits$ will be called an {\em isomorphism of $\mathbb{G}$-structures} on $S$.

nodes.name: Groupoid GStr(S) of G-structures
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S)$ the groupoid formed by $\mathbb{G}$-structures on $S$ and their isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Groupoid GStr^+(S) of orientation-compatible G-structures
nodes.statement: Given an oriented surface $S$, we denote by $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}^+(S)$ the full subcategory in $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S)$ formed by those $\mathbb{G}$-structures which induce the given orientation.

nodes.name: Classification of G-structures on a surface
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] Suppose $\mathbb{G}$ preserves orientation, and let $S$ be an oriented surface. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a1)] For any object $F\in\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}^+(S)$, the group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F)$ is identified with $K$. \item[(a2)] The set of isomorphism classes of objects of $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}^+(S)$ is either empty or a torsor over $H^1(S,K)$. \end{enumerate} \item[(b)] Suppose $\mathbb{G}$ does not preserve orientation, and let $S$ be any surface. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(b1)] For any object $F\in\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S)$, the group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(F)$ is identified with $H^0(S, \underline K^{\operatorname{or}})$. \item[(b2)] The set of isomorphism classes of objects of $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S)$ is either empty, or is a torsor over $H^1(S,\underline K^{\operatorname{or}})$. \item[(b3)] The group $H^0(S, \underline K^{\operatorname{or}})$ is identified with $K$, if $S$ is orientable, and with the 2-torsion subgroup $K_2\subset K$, if $S$ is non-orientable. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Automorphisms of a $\mathbb{G}$-structure are $K$ (twisted by orientation), and isomorphism classes form an $H^1$-torsor if nonempty.
nodes.label: prop:G-structures

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a topological space and \[ 0\to A\longrightarrow\Gamma'\buildrel\pi\over\longrightarrow \Gamma\to 1 \] be an extension of sheaves of groups on $X$ with abelian kernel $A$. Let $P$ be a sheaf of $\Gamma$-torsors on $X$, with associated class $[P]\in H^1(X, \Gamma)$. In this situation, the $\Gamma$-action on $A$ by conjugation gives rise to the twisted form $A^P$, a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ locally isomorphic to $A$. Denote by $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ the category formed by sheaves $P'$ of $\Gamma'$-torsors on $X$ together with a $\pi$-equivariant map $\pi_{P'}: P'\to P$. Morphisms in $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ are isomorphisms of torsors commuting with the projection to $P$. In the described situation, we have: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] Each group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_{\operatorname{Lift}(P)}(P')$ is identified with $H^0(X, A^P)$. \item[(ii)] The set of isomorphism classes of objects of $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ is either empty or is a torsor over $H^1(X, A^P)$. \item[(iii)] If $A$ is central, then there is a natural coboundary map of pointed sets $\delta: H^1(X,\Gamma)\to H^2(X, A)$. In this case $\operatorname{Lift}(P)\neq\emptyset$ if and only if $\delta([P])=0$. \end{enumerate} Now, parts (a1-2) and (b1-2) follow by considering the extensions of sheaves on $S$ obtained from \eqref{eq:group-K} by passing to sheaves of $C^\infty$-sections. Part (b3) follows from Proposition \ref{prop:group-K}(b).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the general theory of lifts of torsors along abelian extensions of sheaves of groups.

nodes.name: Existence of N-spin structures
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an oriented surface and $G=\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)$. If $S$ is noncompact or has nonempty boundary then we have $H^2(S,K) = 0$ so that $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}^+(S)$ is nonempty. If $S$ is compact without boundary, then $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}^+(S)$ is nonempty for $N=2$. This follows by considering the inclusion of short exact sequences of sheaves of groups \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ 0\ar[r]& \underline{\mathbb{Z}/2}\ar[r]\ar[d]^{=}&\underline{S}^1\ar[d] \ar[r]^{z \mapsto z^2} & \underline{S}^1\ar[d]\ar[r] & 1 \\ 0\ar[r]& \underline{\mathbb{Z}/2}\ar[r]&\underline{\widetilde {GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}_2}\ar[r] & \underline {GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}\ar[r] & 1 } \end{equation} where $S^1=SO(2)$. Choosing a Riemannian metric on $S$, we reduce the structure group to $S^1$ and so realize $[\operatorname{Fr}_S]$ as coming from an element of $H^1(S, \underline{S}^1)$. The coboundary map $\delta_{S^1}: H^1(S, \underline S^1)\to H^2(S, \mathbb{Z}/2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ is given by the degree modulo $2$. Since the tangent bundle of a surface of genus $g$ has degree $2g -2$, we have $\delta_{S^1}([\operatorname{Fr}_S]) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $N$-spin structures exist on noncompact or bordered surfaces, and for $N=2$ also on closed ones by a degree computation.

nodes.name: Inclusion of exact sequences for 2-spin structures
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ 0\ar[r]& \underline{\mathbb{Z}/2}\ar[r]\ar[d]^{=}&\underline{S}^1\ar[d] \ar[r]^{z \mapsto z^2} & \underline{S}^1\ar[d]\ar[r] & 1 \\ 0\ar[r]& \underline{\mathbb{Z}/2}\ar[r]&\underline{\widetilde {GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}_2}\ar[r] & \underline {GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}\ar[r] & 1 }
nodes.label: eq;two-seq

nodes.name: G-structured marked surface
nodes.statement: A {\em $\mathbb{G}$-structured marked surface} is a datum consisting of: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] A compact surface $S$ (possibly with boundary). We denote $S^\circ= S-\partial S$ the interior of $S$. \item[(2)] A finite subset $M\subset S$. \item[(3)] A $\mathbb{G}$-structure $F$ on $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Structured diffeomorphism of marked surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $(S,M)$ and $(S', M')$ be two $\mathbb{G}$-structured marked surfaces, with $\mathbb{G}$-structured torsors $F$ and $F'$ respectively. A {\em structured diffeomorphism} $(S,M)\to(S', M')$ is a datum consisting of: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] A diffeomoprhism $\phi: S\to S'$ taking $M$ to $M'$. \item[(2)] A structured diffeomorphism $\widetilde\phi: S-(M\cap S^\circ)\to S'- (M'\cap S'{}^\circ)$ lifting the restriction of $\phi$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Structured diffeomorphism groups Diff^G(S,M)
nodes.statement: For a $\mathbb{G}$-structured marked surface $(S,M)$, we denote by $\operatorname{Diff}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ the group of $\mathbb{G}$-structured self-diffeomorphisms of $(S,M)$, and by $\operatorname{Diff}^\mathbb{G}_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M)$ the subgroup of structured self-diffeomorphisms preserving $M$ pointwise.

nodes.name: Ordinary diffeomorphism groups of a marked surface
nodes.statement: For $\mathbb{G}=GL(2,\mathbb{R})$, we get the ordinary (pure) diffeomorphism group of the marked surface $(S,M)$, which we denote $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$ and $\operatorname{Diff}_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M)$.

nodes.name: Structured diffeomorphism groups cover ordinary ones
nodes.statement: The group $\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits(\pi)=\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits(\pi_{\operatorname{pure}})$ is a discrete abelian group, so that $\pi$ and $\pi_{\operatorname{pure}}$ are unramified coverings. Further, the groups $\operatorname{Im}(\pi)$ and $\operatorname{Im}(\pi_{\operatorname{pure}})$ are unions of connected components of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: The forgetful map from structured to ordinary diffeomorphism groups has discrete abelian kernel and open-closed image.
nodes.label: prop:str-non-str-diff

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.8
nodes.statement_short: Identify the kernel with $\operatorname{Aut}(F)$ and the image with a stabilizer of a discrete set via Proposition 3.4.

nodes.name: G-structured mapping class group
nodes.statement: Let $(S,M)$ be a $\mathbb{G}$-structued marked surface. We define the $\mathbb{G}$-structured mapping class groups as \[ \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) = \pi_0 \operatorname{Diff}^\mathbb{G}(S,M), \quad \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M) =\pi_0 \operatorname{Diff}_{\operatorname{pure}}^\mathbb{G}(S,M). \]

nodes.name: Schottky double
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a compact $C^\infty$-surface with boundary $\partial S$, and $S^\circ = S-\partial S$. The {\em Schottky double} of $S$ is the compact oriented $C^\infty$ surface $S^\#$ without boundary obtained by compatifying $\widetilde{S^\circ}$, the orientation cover of $S^\circ$, by adding one copy of $\partial S$. Thus we have a 2-sheeted covering $\pi: S^\#\to S$, ramified along $\partial S$, and the deck involution $\sigma: S^\#\to S^\#$ of this covering, reversing the orientation and identical on $\partial S$. If $(S,M)$ is a marked surface, we equip $S^\#$ with the subset $M^\#=\pi^{-1}(M)$.

nodes.name: Classical surface
nodes.statement: \cite{seppala} A surface $S$ is called {\em classical}, if $S$ is orientable and $\partial S=\emptyset$, and {\em non-classical} otherwise.

nodes.name: Stable marked surface
nodes.statement: A marked surface $(S,M)$ is called {\em stable}, if: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] $M\neq\emptyset$ and moreover, $M$ meets each component of $\partial S$. \item[(2)] $\chi (S^\# - M^\#) < 0$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Punctures
nodes.statement: For a stable marked surface $(S,M)$ the points of $M$ lying in the interior of $S$, will be called {\em punctures}.

nodes.name: Contractibility of structured diffeomorphism group components
nodes.statement: If $(S,M)$ is a stable $\mathbb{G}$-structured marked surface, then each component of $\operatorname{Diff}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ is contractible.
assumptions: If $(S,M)$ is a stable $\mathbb{G}$-structured marked surface
nodes.label: prop:diff-contract

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.13
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:str-non-str-diff}, the statement reduces to the particular case of $\mathbb{G}=GL(2,\mathbb{R})$ where it translates to the contractibility of each component or, equivalently, of the identity component of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$. This statement is shown in \cite{gramain}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to ordinary diffeomorphism groups via Proposition 3.8 and cite Gramain.

nodes.name: Conformal group embedding Conf(2) in GL(2,R)
nodes.statement: {\operatorname{Conf}}(2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)\ltimes \mathbb{C}^* \subset GL(2, \mathbb{R})
nodes.label: eq:emb-conf

nodes.name: Conformal connective covering G_conf
nodes.statement: We denote \[ p_{\operatorname{conf}}: G_{\operatorname{conf}}\longrightarrow {\operatorname{Conf}}(2) \] the connective covering obtained by restricting $\mathbbm{p}$.

nodes.name: G_conf-structured surface
nodes.statement: Similarly to \S \ref{subsec:c-infty}, by a $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-{\em structured surface} we mean a surface $S$ together with a restriction of the structure group of $\operatorname{Fr}_S$ to $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$. As before, such a structure is a datum of a principal $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-bundle $F_{\operatorname{conf}}$ together with a compatible $P_{\operatorname{conf}}$-equivariant map $F_{\operatorname{conf}}\to\operatorname{Fr}_S$.

nodes.name: Riemann, spin and Klein surfaces as conformal structured surfaces
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})] \item An $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a {\em Riemann surface}, i.e., a 1-dimensional complex manifold $X$ possibly with boundary. More precisely, an isomorphism class of objects of $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}} \operatorname{Str}(S)$ is the same as an almost complex structure $J: T_S\to T_S$, $J^2=-1$, and the automorphism group of any object of $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}} \operatorname{Str}(S)$ is trivial. As well known, all almost complex structures in complex dimension $1$ are integrable. For a Riemann surface $X=(S,J)$ we denote by $\overline X = (S, -J)$ the {\em conjugate} Riemann surface. \item A $\operatorname{Spin}_N(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a triple $(X, \mathcal{L}, \phi)$ where $X$ is a Riemann surface, $\mathcal{L}$ is a line bundle on $X$, and $\phi: \mathcal{L}^{\otimes N}\to\omega_X$ is an isomorphism. Here $\omega_X$ is the canonical line bundle of $X$. For $N=2$, such line bundles $\mathcal{L}$ are traditionally called {\em theta-characteristics}, and a choice of $\mathcal{L}$ is often referred to as a ``spin structure" on $X$, cf. \cite{atiyah}. For ``higher spin structures" on Riemann surfaces ($N>2$), see \cite{jarvis}. \item An $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a {\em Klein surface}, i.e., a surface together with an atlas whose transition maps are conformal but do not necessarily preserve orientation. Such maps are called {\em dianalytic} (i.e., analytic or anti-analytic). Thus a Klein surface does not have to be orientable. See \cite{alling-greenleaf, braun} for more background. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Riemann surface
nodes.statement: An $SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a {\em Riemann surface}, i.e., a 1-dimensional complex manifold $X$ possibly with boundary.

nodes.name: Klein surface
nodes.statement: An $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured surface is a {\em Klein surface}, i.e., a surface together with an atlas whose transition maps are conformal but do not necessarily preserve orientation.

nodes.name: Conformal G-structures as products
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] For any surface $S$ we have a natural identification of groupoids \[ G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S) \simeq \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S) \times O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}} \operatorname{Str}(S). \] \item[(b)] The automorphism group of any object of $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}} \operatorname{Str}(S)$ is trivial. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structures are pairs of a $\mathbb{G}$-structure and a conformal structure; conformal structures have no automorphisms.
nodes.label: prop:prod-of-grpds

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.15
nodes.statement: (a) By definition, we have \[ G_{\operatorname{conf}} = \mathbb{G} \times_{GL(2,\mathbb{R})} O(2)_{{\operatorname{conf}}} \] where $O(2)_{{\operatorname{conf}}}={\operatorname{Conf}}(2)$. So given a $\mathbb{G}$-structure $F\to \operatorname{Fr}_S$ and an $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure $F^{O(2)}_{\operatorname{conf}} \to\operatorname{Fr}_S$, we obtain a $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure by forming the fiber product \[ F_{\operatorname{conf}} \,\,=\,\, F\times_{\operatorname{Fr}_S} F^{O(2)}_{\operatorname{conf}} \] which is a principal $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-bundle. We leave the remaining details to the reader. (b) Follows because $O(2)_{{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is a subgroup of $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.statement_short: Fiber product of the two structures; triviality since $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\subset GL(2,\mathbb{R})$.

nodes.name: Schottky double of a Riemann surface
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a Riemann surface. Then $X^\# = X\cup_{\partial X} \overline X$.
nodes.section: 3.2.2 Klein surfaces and algebraic curves over $\mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Klein surfaces, symmetric Riemann surfaces and real curves
nodes.statement: The Schottky double construction establishes an equivalence between the following categories: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Non-classical Klein surfaces $X$. \item[(ii)] Pairs $(Y,\sigma)$ where $Y$ is a compact Riemann surface without boundary and $\sigma: Y\to Y$ is an anti-holomorphic involution. \item[(iii)] Smooth projective algebraic curves over $\mathbb{R}$. \qed \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3.2.2 Klein surfaces and algebraic curves over $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement_short: Schottky double gives equivalences between non-classical Klein surfaces, symmetric Riemann surfaces and smooth projective real curves.

nodes.name: Symmetric Riemann surface
nodes.statement: Pairs $(Y,\sigma)$ as in (ii) are known as {\em symmetric Riemann surfaces}.
nodes.section: 3.2.2 Klein surfaces and algebraic curves over $\mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Space Riem^+(S) of complex structures
nodes.statement: We denote by $\operatorname{Riem}^+(S)$ the space of all complex structures on $S$ compatible with the orientation.
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces

nodes.name: Identity component Diff(S,M)_e
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)_e$ be the identity component of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$.
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces

nodes.name: Classical Teichmuller space
nodes.statement: The classical {\em Teichm\"uller space} of $(S,M)$ is defined as the quotient \[ \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)_e \backslash \operatorname{Riem}^+(S). \]
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces

nodes.name: Classical Teichmuller space
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be the genus of $S$ and suppose that $(S,M)$ is stable, i.e., $2g-2+|M|>0$. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ has a natural structure of a complex manifold of dimension $3g-3+|M|$. As a $C^\infty$-manifold, it is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space. \item[(b)] Let $\sigma:S\to S$ be an orientation reversing involution preserving $M$ as a set. Conjugation with $\sigma$ defines an anti-holomorphic involution \[ \sigma_{\operatorname{Teich}}: \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M). \qed \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ is a complex manifold of dimension $3g-3+|M|$ diffeomorphic to Euclidean space, with anti-holomorphic involutions from orientation reversing involutions.

nodes.name: Space Klein(S) of conformal structures
nodes.statement: Denote by $\operatorname{Klein}(S)$ the space of all possible conformal structures on $S$.
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces

nodes.name: Teichmuller space of a stable marked surface
nodes.statement: The {\em Teichm\"uller space} of $(S,M)$ is defined by \[ \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)\backslash \operatorname{Klein}(S). \]
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces

nodes.name: Teichmuller spaces of marked Klein surfaces
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] If $S$ is classical (i.e., orientable without boundary), then the space $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is the disjoint union of two connected components, corresponding to the two orientations of $S$. Each component is canonically identified with the corresponding classical Teichm\"uller space $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$. \item[(b1)] Suppose $S$ is non-classical, let $\pi: S^\#\to S$ be its Schottky double with involution $\sigma$, and let $M^\#=\pi^{-1}(M)$. Let $g^\#$ be the genus of $S^\#$. Then \[ \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) = (\operatorname{Teich}^+(S^\#, M^\#))^{\sigma_{\operatorname{Teich}}} \] is the fixed point locus of the anti-holomorphic involution $\sigma_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. In particular, it is a real analytic manifold of dimension $3g^\#-3+|M^\#|$. \item[(b2)] Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, let $\varpi: \widetilde S\to S$ be its orientation cover with the orientation reversing deck involution $\tau$, and let $\widetilde M=\varpi^{-1}(M)$. Then \[ \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) = (\operatorname{Teich}^+(\widetilde S, \widetilde M))^{\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}} \] is the fixed point locus of the involution $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. \item[(c)] In the situation (b1), the manifold $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is two copies of the classical one for classical $S$, and otherwise the fixed locus of an involution on the Teichmüller space of the double, a Euclidean space.
nodes.label: thm:klein-teich

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.19
nodes.statement: Parts (a), (b1-2) are obvious. Part (c) was proved by Natanzon \cite{natanzon} for $\partial S = M=\emptyset$ and Sepp\"al\"a \cite{seppala} for $M=\emptyset$. The extension to the case $M\neq\emptyset$ is can be done by the same methods.
nodes.section: 3.2.3 Teichm\"uller spaces of marked Klein surfaces
nodes.statement_short: Parts (a),(b) are direct; (c) by Natanzon and Seppälä's methods.

nodes.name: G_conf-structured marked surface
nodes.statement: A $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-{\em structured marked surface} is a datum consisting of: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] A conformal surface $S$. \item[(2)] A finite subset $M\subset S$. \item[(3)] A $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure on $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$ compatible with the conformal structure restricted from $S$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Groupoid of conformal G-structures on a marked surface
nodes.statement: Given a $C^\infty$ marked surface $(S,M)$, we have a topological groupoid $G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S,M)$ formed by pairs consisting of a conformal structure on $S$ and a compatible $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure on $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$.

nodes.name: Product decomposition of conformal structure groupoid
nodes.statement: G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S,M)\,\,\simeq \,\, \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))\times O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S).
nodes.label: eq:prod-str

nodes.name: Moduli spaces of G_conf-structured surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $(S, M)$ be a stable marked surface. The {\em moduli spaces} of $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structures on $(S,M)$ are defined as the groupoid quotients \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S,M)), \\ \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}_{\operatorname{pure}} (S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Diff}_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S,M). \end{gathered} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Moduli spaces of G_conf-structured surfaces
nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S,M)), \\ \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}_{\operatorname{pure}} (S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Diff}_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash G_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S,M). \end{gathered}

nodes.name: Moduli space as groupoid of structured surfaces
nodes.statement: Equivalently, $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M)$ can be seen as the groupoid formed by all $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured marked surfaces of topological type $(S,M)$ and by their structured diffeomorphisms.

nodes.name: Deligne-Mumford moduli of curves as oriented case
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a finite set and suppose that $2g-2+|M|>0$. Let $\mathcal{M}(g,M)$ be the Deligne-Mumford moduli stack formed by smooth projective algebraic curves $X$ of genus $g$ together with an embedding $M\hookrightarrow X$. Let $(S,M)$ be a classical marked surface of genus $g$. Any choice of an orientation of $S$ identifies $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}_{{\operatorname{pure}}}(S,M)$ with the groupoid (orbifold) of $\mathbb{C}$-points $\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C})$. Change of orientation corresponds to the action of $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R})$ on $\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C})$ which comes from the fact that $\mathcal{M}(g,M)$ is defined over $\mathbb{R}$ (in fact, over $\mathbb{Q}$). The orbifold $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is therefore the quotient of $\mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C})$ by the symmetric group of $M$. As is well known, \[ \mathcal{M}(g,M)(\mathbb{C}) = \operatorname{Mod}^+_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M) \] is the quotient of the topological cell $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ by the mapping class group of orientation preserving diffeomorphisms fixing all points of $M$. In what follows, we realize a general $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M)$ in terms of quotients of cells by discrete groups.

nodes.name: Topological moduli groupoid M^G(S,M)
nodes.statement: Let $(S,M)$ be stable, and define \begin{equation} \mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)\bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ)) \simeq \operatorname{Mod}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ)) \end{equation} as the ``topological" analog of the moduli space, in which we consider $\mathbb{G}$ instead of $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$ as a structure group.

nodes.name: Topological moduli groupoid M^G(S,M)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)\bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ)) \simeq \operatorname{Mod}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))
nodes.label: eq:top-moduli

nodes.name: Moduli space as union of Teichmuller quotients
nodes.statement: We have a homotopy equivalence of topological groupoids \[ \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \simeq \coprod_{ \{F\} \in \mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S_F, M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) \] and a similar identification of $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}_{\operatorname{pure}}(S,M)$. Here $\{ F\}$ runs over isomorphism classes of objects of $\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$, and $S_F$ is the $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface corresponding to $F$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M)$ is a disjoint union over $\mathbb{G}$-structures of quotients of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ by structured mapping class groups.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.23
nodes.statement: Using \eqref{eq:prod-str}, we have \begin{align*} \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) & = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \bigl( \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ)) \times O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\bigr)\\ & = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \biggl\backslash \hskip -.25cm \biggl\backslash \coprod_{ \{F\}\in \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))} O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\\ & = \coprod _{ \{F\}\in \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))} \biggl( \operatorname{Stab}(F) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\biggr). \end{align*} Note that at the bottom of last coproduct the quotient by $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$ is $\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$. At the same time, $\operatorname{Stab}(F)$ is the union of connected components of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$, in particular, $\operatorname{Stab}(F)_e = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)_e$. Therefore the above coproduct can be identified with \[ \begin{gathered} \coprod_{ \{F\}\in\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \pi_0 (\operatorname{Stab}(F)) \biggl\backslash \hskip -.25cm \biggl\backslash \biggl( \operatorname{Stab}(F)_e \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\biggr)\,\,= \\ =\,\, \coprod_{ \{F\} \in\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S_F, M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) \end{gathered} \] as claimed. In the last identification, we identified the topological groupoid $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)$ with the topological space $\operatorname{Klein}(S)$ of its isomorphism classes. This is possible because all automorphism groups of objects in this groupoid are trivial by Proposition \ref{prop:prod-of-grpds}(b).
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the quotient over orbits of $\mathbb{G}$-structures and use that stabilizers are unions of components.

nodes.name: Graph (halfedge formalism)
nodes.statement: A {\em graph} $\Gamma$ is a pair of sets $(H,V)$ equipped with \begin{itemize} \item an involution $\tau: H \to H$, \item a map $s: H \to V$. \end{itemize} The elements of $H$ are called {\em halfedges} of $\Gamma$, the fixed points of $\tau$ are called {\em external halfedges}, and the nonfixed points of $\tau$ are called {\em internal halfedges}. The $2$-element orbits of $\tau$, which are hence comprised of a pair of internal halfedges, are called {\em edges}. The elements of $V$ are called the {\em vertices} of $\Gamma$. Given a vertex $v \in V$, we define the set $H(v) = s^{-1}(v)$ of {\em halfedges incident to $v$}. The cardinality $|H(v)|$ is called the valency of $v$.

nodes.name: Incidence category and incidence diagram of a graph
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a graph. The {\em incidence category} $I(\Gamma)$ of $\Gamma$ has, as objects, all the vertices and edges of $\Gamma$ with a non-identity morphism $s(h) \to \{h,\tau(h)\}$ for every internal halfedge $h$. The {\em incidence diagram of $\Gamma$} is the functor \[ I_{\Gamma}: I(\Gamma) \longrightarrow {\mathcal Set} \] given on objects by assigning to a vertex $v$ the set $H(v)$ and to an edge $e$ with half-edges $h,h'$, the $2$-element set $\{h,h'\}$. To a morphism $s(h) \to \{h,h'\}$ we associate the map of sets $H(s(h)) \to \{h,h'\}$ given by mapping $h$ to $h'$ and collapsing the remaining halfedges in $H(s(h))$ (denoted by A in Fig. \ref{fig:F1}) to $h$.

nodes.name: Compact graph
