nodes.statement: We say a graph is {\em compact} if all its halfedges are internal.

nodes.name: Realization of a graph
nodes.statement: Given a graph $\Gamma$, we define its {\em realization} $|\Gamma| = |\operatorname{N}(I(\Gamma)|$ to be the geometric realization of its incidence category. We denote by $\partial |\Gamma|\subset|\Gamma|$ the set of 1-valent vertices and by $|\Gamma|^\circ$ the complement $|\Gamma| - \partial|\Gamma|$.

nodes.name: Vertex and midpoint cells of the realization
nodes.statement: Note that the realization $|\Gamma|$ comes equipped with two kinds of $0$-cells. On the one hand, we have a $0$-cell for each vertex $v$ of $\Gamma$, on the other hand, we have a $0$-cell $m(e)$ for each edge $e$ of $\Gamma$ which can be regarded as a chosen midpoint of the geometric edge which connects the two vertices of $\Gamma$ incident to $e$, see Figure \ref{fig:F1}.
nodes.label: rem:midpoint

nodes.name: G-structure on a graph
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a graph and let ${\mathcal G}$ be a small category equipped with a functor ${\mathcal G} \to {\mathcal Set}$. A {\em ${\mathcal G}$-structure on $\Gamma$} is a lift \[ \xymatrix{ & {\mathcal G} \ar[d] \\ I(\Gamma) \ar[r]^{I_{\Gamma}} \ar[ur]^{\widetilde{I_{\Gamma}}} & {\mathcal Set} } \] of the incidence diagram of $\Gamma$ to ${\mathcal G}$.
nodes.label: defi:ggraph

nodes.name: Ribbon, Moebius, framed and N-spin graphs
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item A graph with a $\Lambda$-structure is called a {\em ribbon graph}. Explicitly, a $\Lambda$-structure on a graph $\Gamma$ is the datum of a cyclic order on the $H(v)$ for each vertex $v\in V$. Each set $\{h,h'\}$ of half-edges of any edge $e$ has a trivial cyclic order, since it has cardinality 2. Thus, our definition reduces to the usual one \cite{penner:book}. \item A graph with a $\Xi$-structure is called a {\em M\"obius graph}. Explicitly, a $\Xi$-structure on a graph $\Gamma$ consists, first, of a dihedral order on each $H(v)$ and, second, of identification of the orientation torsors \[ O(H(v))\buildrel\sim\over \longleftarrow O(e)\buildrel\sim\over \longrightarrow O(H(v')) \] for each edge $e$ with vertices $v$ and $v'$ (the case $v=v'$ is allowed). This structure is equivalent to the (somewhat more cumbersome) concept of a M\"obius graph defined in terms of ``ribbon graphs with $\mathbb{Z}/2$-grading on edges" as in \cite{braun, mulase-waldron, mulase-yu}. \item A graph with a $\Lambda_{\infty}$-structure is called a {\em framed graph}. \item A graph with a $\Lambda_N$-structure is called an {\em $N$-spin graph}. Very recently, surfaces with 2-spin structure were studied, from a combinatorial point of view by Novak and Runkel \cite{novak-runkel}. They introduced a concept of a combinatorial spin structure on a triangulation $T$ of a surface $S$. Such a structure equips the dual graph of $T$ with a $\Lambda_2$-structure in our sense. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: defi:exggraphs

nodes.name: Ribbon graph
nodes.statement: A graph with a $\Lambda$-structure is called a {\em ribbon graph}.

nodes.name: Moebius graph
nodes.statement: A graph with a $\Xi$-structure is called a {\em M\"obius graph}.

nodes.name: Framed graph
nodes.statement: A graph with a $\Lambda_{\infty}$-structure is called a {\em framed graph}.

nodes.name: N-spin graph
nodes.statement: A graph with a $\Lambda_N$-structure is called an {\em $N$-spin graph}.

nodes.name: Circle of directions
nodes.statement: For a 2-dimensional $\mathbb{R}$-vector space $V$, we denote by \[ C(V) \,\,=\,\, (V-\{0\})/\mathbb{R}^*_{>0} \] the circle of directions of $V$.

nodes.name: Embedding of a graph into a surface
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a surface. By an {\em embedding} of a graph $\Gamma$ into $S$ we mean an injective, continous map $\gamma: |\Gamma| \to S$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\gamma(|\Gamma|^\circ)$ is contained in the interior of $S$, and $\gamma(\partial|\Gamma|)\subset\partial S$. \item $\gamma$ is smooth along every edge of $|\Gamma|$. \item For every vertex $x$ of $|\Gamma|$ (corresponding to a vertex or and edge of $\Gamma$), the tangent directions of the edge germs on $S$ which leave $\gamma(x)$, are distinct. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: exa:embedding

nodes.name: Embedded graphs inherit Delta-G-structures
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a surface with a $\mathbb{G}$-structure. An embedding of a graph $\Gamma$ into $S$ endows $\Gamma$ with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a surface with a $\mathbb{G}$-structure.
conclusions: An embedding of a graph $\Gamma$ into $S$ endows $\Gamma$ with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure.
nodes.label: prop:emb-graph-str

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.8
nodes.statement_short: Structure tangent direction circles via the $\mathbb{G}$-structure and Corollary 2.15. Incidence morphisms come from a canonical lift of parallel transport through the covering of homeomorphisms.

nodes.name: Embedded graphs as ribbon, Moebius, framed and N-spin graphs
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}=\Lambda$. If $\Gamma$ be embedded into an oriented surface $S$, then it is classical that $\Gamma$ is canonically a ribbon graph. Explicitly, each $H(v)$ has a cyclic order from the embedding into the oriented circle $C(T_{\gamma(v)} S)$, while the set of half-edges of any edge has a unique cyclic order since it has cardinality $2$. \item Suppose ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}=\Xi$. Let $\Gamma$ be embedded into an unoriented surface $S$. Then $\Gamma$ naturally admits the structure of a M\"obius graph. The set $H(v)$ of half-edges incident to $v$ inherits a dihedral order from the embedding into the circle $C(T_{\gamma(v)} S)$. The set $\{h,h'\}$ of half-edges of an edge $e$ is made into a dihedral set by looking at the orientation cover $\varpi: \widetilde \to S$: we define the orientation torsor $O(\{h,h'\})$ of this set to be the set of sections of $\pi$ over the image, under $\gamma$, of the interior of $|e|$. Finally, we have to provide a lift of the incidence map $i: H(s(h)) \to \{h,h'\}$ to a morphism of dihedrally ordered sets. Note that, by the path lifting property of the orientation cover $\pi$, the orientation torsors of $H(s(h))$ and $\{h,h'\}$ are canonically identified. For every choice of orientation, there is now a unique linear order on $i^{-1}(h')$ compatible with the corresponding cyclic order of $H(s(h))$. These two linear orders are opposite providing $i$ with the structure of a morphism in ${\Xi}$. \item Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}={\Lambda}_\infty$. Assume that $\Gamma$ is embedded into a framed surface $S$. This means, in particular, that $S$ is oriented so that we have a principal $GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})$-bundle $\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$ of positive frames on $S$. Further, we are given a principal $\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$-bundle $\widetilde\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$ covering $\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$. Thus, each fiber of $\widetilde\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$ is a universal cover of the corresponding fiber of $\operatorname{Fr}^+_S$. Let \[ B^+ \,\,=\,\, \biggl\{ \begin{pmatrix} a&b\\0&c \end{pmatrix}\,\in GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})\bigl\| \,\, a,c >0\biggr\}. \] Then $B^+\backslash GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})=S^1$ is the circle of directions of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Therefore $B^+\backslash \operatorname{Fr}^+_S=C(T_S)$ is the circle bundle of directions of $T_S$. Further, $B^+$, being contractible, lifts canonically to a subgroup $\widetilde B^+\subset\widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}$. The quotient $\widetilde B^+\backslash \widetilde{GL^+(2,\mathbb{R})}\simeq\mathbb{R}$ is the universal covering of $S^1$. So each fiber $\widetilde C(T_xS)= \widetilde B^+\backslash \widetilde\operatorname{Fr}^+_{S,x}$ is an oriented real line, equipped with the projection $\pi_x: \widetilde C(T_xS)\to C(T_xS)$ exhibiting it as a universal covering of $C(T_xS)$. Therefore, for each vertex $v\in\Gamma$ the preimage of $H(v)\subset C(T_{\gamma(v)}S)$ is naturally a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor, thus giving a paracyclic order on $H(v)$. Similarly for each edge $\{h,h'\}$. We leave remaining details to the reader. \item Assume that $\Gamma$ is embedded into a surface $S$ which has an $N$-spin structure. Then, similarly to (3) , we consider an $N$-fold covering $\pi_x: \widetilde C_N(T_xS)\to C(T_xS)$ for each $x\in S$. Taking $\pi_{\gamma(v)}^{-1}(H(v))$, we make each $H(v)$ into an $N$-cyclic set, and similarly for each set $\{h,h'\}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Weak equivalence of graphs
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$ be graphs. A {\em weak equivalence} between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ is a functor $\varphi: I(\Gamma) \to I(\Gamma')$ of incidence categories such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\varphi$ induces a bijection of the sets of vertices of valency $1$, \item the induced map $|\varphi|: |I(\Gamma)| \to |I(\Gamma')|$ is homotopy equivalence. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces

nodes.name: Weak equivalence of structured graphs and the category Delta-G-Graph
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$ be ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs. A {\em weak equivalence} $\varphi: \Gamma \to \Gamma'$ of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs is a weak equivalence of underlying graphs together with a lift of the pullback morphism $\varphi^* I_{\Gamma'} \to I_{\Gamma}$ to a morphism of ${\mathcal G}$-diagrams $\varphi^* \widetilde{I_{\Gamma'}} \to \widetilde{I_{\Gamma}}$. We define ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}$ to be the category with objects given by (compact) ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs without vertices of valency $2$ and morphisms given by weak equivalences.
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces
nodes.label: def:weak-eq-str-graphs

nodes.name: Contractions of structured graphs
nodes.statement: Sometimes we will refer to weak equivalences of structured graphs as {\em contractions}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces

nodes.name: Structured graphs classify structured mapping class groups
nodes.statement: The topological realization $|N({\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph})|$ is a classifying space of $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces so that we have a homotopy equivalence \[ |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \simeq \coprod_{(S,M)} B\, \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M), \] where the coproduct is taken over all topological types of stable marked $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces $(S,M)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces
nodes.statement_short: The nerve of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-$\operatorname{Graph}$ is homotopy equivalent to $\coprod B\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ over stable marked $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces.
nodes.label: thm:g-graph

nodes.name: Spanning graph and poset P(S,M)
nodes.statement: Let $(S,M)$ be a stable marked surface. A {\em spanning graph} for $(S,M)$ is a graph $\Gamma$ together with an embedding $\gamma: |\Gamma|\to S$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $\gamma$ is a homotopy equivalence. \item The restriction of $\gamma$ defines a homotopy equivalence between $\partial |\Gamma|$ (a finite set of points) and $\partial S - M$ (a finite set of open intervals). \end{enumerate} We define the category $P(S,M)$ whose objects are isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$ and with a unique morphism $[\Gamma] \to [\Gamma']$ if $[\Gamma']$ is obtained from $[\Gamma]$ by collapsing a forest. Note that $P(S,M)$ is in fact a poset.
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces

nodes.name: Contractibility of the spanning graph poset
nodes.statement: For any stable marked surface $(S,M)$ the poset $P(S,M)$ is contractible.
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces
nodes.label: thm:graph-contr

nodes.name: Functor rho from P(S,M) to structured graphs
nodes.statement: Assume that $(S,M)$ carries a $\mathbb{G}$-structure. We then have a functor \begin{equation} \rho: P(S,M) \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \end{equation} which chooses for a graph $(\Gamma,\gamma)$ in every isotopy class and associates to it the ${\mathcal G}$-structure on $\Gamma$ induced from the embedding $\gamma$ (Proposition \ref {prop:emb-graph-str}).
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces

nodes.name: Functor rho from spanning graphs to structured graphs
nodes.statement: \rho: P(S,M) \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces
nodes.label: eq:rho

nodes.name: Theorem 4.12 as an equivalence of a semidirect product
nodes.statement: Further, the structured mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)$ acts on $P(S,M)$ and we can form the semidirect product \[ \operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M) \ltimes P(S,M) \] as defined in Definition \ref{defi:semidirect}. The proof of Theorem \ref{thm:g-graph} amounts to the statement that the functor $\rho$ extends to an equivalence of categories \[ \widetilde{\rho}: \operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M) \ltimes P(S,M) \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}, \] see Theorem \ref{thm:decomp}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Structured graphs and mapping class groups of structured surfaces

nodes.name: Augmented Delta-G-structured graph
nodes.statement: An {\em augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph} is a possibly noncompact ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph $\Gamma$ equipped with \begin{itemize} \item for every external halfedge $e \in H(v)$, an {\em augmentation map} $\varphi_e: H(v) \to [1]$ of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets, satisfying $\varphi_e^{-1}(\varphi(e)) = \{e\}$, \end{itemize} such that every vertex of $\Gamma$ has valency $\ge 2$.

nodes.name: Incoming and outgoing halfedges
nodes.statement: Given an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph $\Gamma$, we obtain a partition of the set of external halfedges into {\em incoming} ($\varphi_e(e) = 1$) and {\em outgoing} ($\varphi_e(e) = 0$).

nodes.name: Contraction of augmented structured graphs
nodes.statement: A {\em contraction} of augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs is a contraction of the underlying ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs which commutes with the augmentations.

nodes.name: Noncompact interval
nodes.statement: A noncompact {\em interval} is a connected graph with two external halfedges and all vertices of valency $2$:

nodes.name: Augmented structured interval diagram
nodes.statement: [1] \overset{\varphi_e}{\longleftarrow} H(v) \overset{\varphi_f}{\longrightarrow} [1]
nodes.label: eq:interval

nodes.name: Category Tr(1) of augmented structured intervals
nodes.statement: We define $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ to be the category of augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured intervals with external halfedges labelled by $0$ (outgoing) and $1$ (incoming) and with contractions as morphisms.

nodes.name: Set of components pi_0 Tr(1)
nodes.statement: We denote by $\pi_0\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ the set of isomorphism classes in the groupoid completion of $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ so that two objects $\Gamma$,$\Gamma'$ are in the same class if and only if there exists a chain of zigzag contractions \[ \Gamma \longleftarrow \Gamma_1 \longrightarrow \Gamma_2 \longleftarrow \dots \longrightarrow \Gamma'. \]

nodes.name: Monoid of structured intervals
nodes.statement: The monoid $\pi_0 \operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ can be canonically identified with the group $\mathfrak{G}_1^0$.
nodes.statement_short: Components of augmented structured intervals form the group $\mathfrak{G}_1^0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.16
nodes.statement: Given an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured interval as in \eqref{eq:interval}, note that $\varphi_e$ and $\varphi_f$ are isomorphisms in ${\mathcal G}$. Using $\varphi_e$ to identify $H(v)$ with $[1]$, we obtain that the augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-strutured interval is isomorphic to \[ [1] \overset{\operatorname{id}}{\longleftarrow} [1] \overset{g}{\longrightarrow} [1] \] where $g$ is an automorphism of $[1]$ which induces the identity on the underlying set $\{0,1\}$. Therefore, we have $g \in \mathfrak{G}_1^0$ where $\mathfrak{G}_1^0$ denotes the kernel of the map $\lambda: \mathfrak{G}_1 \to S_2$ from Proposition \ref{prop:forget}. It is immediate to verify that this identitication is compatible with the group law on $\mathfrak{G}_1^0$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the augmentation and read off an automorphism of $[1]$ over the identity.

nodes.name: Structured intervals for planar crossed simplicial groups
nodes.statement: For a planar crossed simplicial group, the monoid $\pi_0 \operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ is canonically isomorphic to the group $\mathfrak{G}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: For planar $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ the interval monoid is $\mathfrak{G}_0$.

nodes.name: Category Tr(n) of augmented structured trees
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ denote the category of augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured trees with external halfedges labelled by $0,1,\dots,n$ such that the halfedge $0$ is outgoing and all remaining halfedges are incoming. The morphisms in $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ are given by contractions of augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs.

nodes.name: Operad components P(n)
nodes.statement: We define $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ to be the set $\pi_0 \operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ of isomorphism classes in the groupoid completion of $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$.

nodes.name: Operad of augmented structured trees
nodes.statement: Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a crossed simplicial group. \begin{enumerate} \item The action of $S_n$ on $P_\mathcal{G}(n)$ by relabelling the incoming external halfedges and the maps $\{ m_{a_1, \dots, a_n} \}$ make $P_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}= \{P_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(n)\}_{n\geq 1}$ an operad in the category of sets. \item Assume that ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is planar. Then algebras over $P_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ are precisely monoids with a twisted action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ in the sense of \S \ref{section:semiconstant}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Augmented structured trees form a set operad whose algebras, for planar $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$, are monoids with twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action.
nodes.label: prop:Gc-operad

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.18
nodes.statement: Part (1) is clear. We show (2). Given an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured tree $\Gamma$ in $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ with augmented incidence diagram $I(\Gamma) \to {\mathcal G}$, we first argue that we can contract all internal edges to obtain a corolla. To this end, we note that, given an internal edge $\{e,e'\}$ incident to vertices $v$ and $v'$, the corresponding diagram \[ H(v) \longrightarrow \{e,e'\} \longleftarrow H(v') \] has a limit in ${\mathcal G}$ whose underlying set is given by $(H(v)\setminus \{e\}) \cup (H(v') \setminus \{e'\})$. This holds for all planar crossed simplicial groups and can be verified using the topological model of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ from \S \ref{sec:topmodel}. We can use the cone diagram of this limit in ${\mathcal G}$ to produce a morphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma \to \Gamma'$ which collapses the edge $\{e,e'\}$. After collapsing all internal edges of $\Gamma$, we obtain an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla $\Gamma_0$. Using the labels we can identify the set $H(v)$ of halfedges incident to the single vertex of $\Gamma_0$ with $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. We can find an isomorphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $f: (\{0,1,\dots,n\}, {\mathcal O}) \cong [n]$ and since, for planar crossed simplicial groups, $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts (simply) transitively on $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([0],[n])$ we may assume that $f$ maps $0$ to $0$. Therefore, after permuting the labels $1,2, \dots, n$, we may assume that $H(v) = [n]$. Every morphism $[n] \to [1]$ such that $\varphi^{-1}(0) = \{0\}$ (corresponding to the outgoing halfedge labeled $0$) can be written as a composite $\varphi g$ where $\varphi: [n] \to [1]$ is the morphism in $\Delta$ which maps $0$ to $0$ and all remaining elements to $1$, and $g \in \operatorname{Stab}(0) \subset \mathfrak{G}_n$. Therefore, we can assume that the augmentation $H(v) = [n] \to [1]$ of the single outgoing halfedge $0$ is given by $\varphi$. For every $1 \le i \le n$, the subset of $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([n],[1])$ given by those morphisms such that $\varphi^{-1}(1) = \{i\}$ forms a torsor under the action of $\mathfrak{G}_1^0 \cong \mathfrak{G}_0$. Note that this action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ is precisely the operadic action of the monoid $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ on the incoming halfedges. Therefore, the collection of isomorphism classes of labelled augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corollas forms a torsor under the action of \[ \underbrace{P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1) \times P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1) \times \dots \times P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)}_n \times S_{n}. \] We will now trivialize this torsor, for every $n$, by choosing a specific ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla in such a way that these chosen $n$-corollas are closed under operadic composition (for $n>1$). To this end, choose a duality functor $D: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ and consider the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ [1] \ar[drr]_{\{0,1\}}& [1] \ar[dr]^{\{1,2\}} & \dots & [1] \ar[dl]^{\{n-1,n\}}\\ & & [n] & \\ & & [1]\ar[u]^{\{0,n\}} & } \] in $\Delta \subset {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ and apply $D$ to obtain the incidence diagram of a labeled augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla which we define to be our chosen trivialization. It is easy to verify that, due to the functoriality of $D$, the collection of corollas thus obtained is closed under operadic composition. This exhibits a copy of the associative operad $\operatorname{Ass}$ in $P$ such that every element of $P$ can be uniquely expressed as an element of $\operatorname{Ass}$ precomposed with elements of the monoid $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ acting on the incoming halfedges. An explicit computation of the action of $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ on the outgoing halfedges of $\operatorname{Ass}$ in terms of the actions on the incoming halfedges implies the claim that $P$ parametrizes algebras with twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action.
nodes.statement_short: Contract trees to corollas and trivialize the torsor of labelled corollas by a copy of the associative operad. The key step chooses corollas via a duality functor so they are closed under composition.

nodes.name: Topological operad of structured trees
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{prop:Gc-operad} can be enhanced by considering the geometric realization of the categories $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(n)$ instead of the set $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ of its connected components. In this way, we obtain an operad $\operatorname{N}\operatorname{Tr}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ in the category of topological spaces which describes $A_\infty$-monoids with a twisted coherent action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$.

nodes.name: Modular operadic interpretation
nodes.statement: The results of this section suggest that augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured {\em graphs} can be interpreted in modular operadic terms generalizing the well-known approaches to $2$-dimensional topological field theories in the cyclic and dihedral cases (cf. \cite{costello-TFT, braun}). We leave the systematic treatment of these generalizations to future work.

nodes.name: d-cell
nodes.statement: By a $d$-{\em cell} we mean a topological space $\sigma$ homeomorphic to an open ball $B^d \subset \mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.name: d-orbicell
nodes.statement: By a $d$-{\em orbicell} we mean a topological groupoid equivalent to $D\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash\sigma$ where $\sigma\simeq B^d$ is a $d$-cell and $D$ is a discrete group acting on $\sigma$ via a homomorphism $\phi: D\to{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(\sigma)$ whose image is identified with a finite group of linear transformations of $B^d$.

nodes.name: Orbicell decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a topological groupoid. An {\em orbicell decomposition} of $X$ is a finite filtration \[ \mathcal{X} = \bigl( \mathcal{X}_0\subset\mathcal{X}_1 \subset\cdots\subset \mathcal{X}_n = X) \] of $X$ by closed topological subgroupoids $\mathcal{X}_d$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] Each $\mathcal{X}_d$ is a full subcategory in $X$. \item[(2)] Each component of $\mathcal{X}_d-\mathcal{X}_{d-1}$ is a disjoint union of $d$-orbicells. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Orbicell decomposition from an equivariant cell decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be a topological space with a cell decomposition ${\mathcal Y}$. Let $D$ be a discrete group acting on $Y$, preserving ${\mathcal Y}$ and such that for each cell $\sigma$ of ${\mathcal Y}$ the stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}(\sigma)$ acting on $\sigma$, makes $\operatorname{Stab}(\sigma)\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash\sigma$ into an orbicell. Then the groupoid $D\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash Y$ has an orbicell decomposition into orbicells $\operatorname{Stab}(\sigma)\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash\sigma$ where $\sigma$ runs over orbits of $D$ on the set of cells of ${\mathcal Y}$.
nodes.label: ex:regular-cell

nodes.name: Regular cell decomposition
nodes.statement: Recall that for ordinary spaces (not groupoids) $Y$ there is a concept of a {\em regular cell decomposition} which is a cell decomposition ${\mathcal Y}$ such that the closure of each $d$-cell $\sigma$ of ${\mathcal Y}$ is homeomorphic to a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (whose boundary is therefore a $(d-1)$-sphere with further cell decomposition induced by ${\mathcal Y}$).

nodes.name: Quotient-regular orbicell decomposition
nodes.statement: An orbicell decomposition $\mathcal{X}$ of a topological groupoid $X$ is called {\em quotient-regular}, if there is an equivalence of $X$ with a quotient groupoid $D\backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash Y$ and a regular $D$-invariant cell decomposition ${\mathcal Y}$ of $Y$ as in Example \ref{ex:regular-cell}, which induces $\mathcal{X}$.

nodes.name: Cell category Cell(X)
nodes.statement: For a quotient-regular cell decomposition $\mathcal{X}$ we have a category ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})$ whose objects are cells of ${\mathcal Y}$ and morphisms are induced by action of $D$ and inclusion of cells.

nodes.name: Classifying space of the cell category
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{X}$ is a quotient-regular orbicell decomposition of $X$, then the classifying space of the (non-topological) category ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})$ is homotopy equivalent to the classifying space of $X$ as a topological category. \qed
assumptions: If $\mathcal{X}$ is a quotient-regular orbicell decomposition of $X$
nodes.label: prop:orbicell-cell

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.12 (via Theorem 4.25)
nodes.statement: We now prove the following fact which, in virtue of Proposition \ref {prop:orbicell-cell}, implies Theorem \ref{thm:g-graph}.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 4.25 plus Proposition 4.24 give the classifying space statement.

nodes.name: Orbicell decomposition of structured moduli spaces
nodes.statement: Consider the orbifold \[ \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}} \,\,=\,\,\coprod_{(S,M)} \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \] where $(S,M)$ runs over all possible topological types of stable marked surfaces. Then $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ has a quotient-regular orbicell decomposition $\mathcal{X}$ such that we have an equivalence of categories ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}$.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces
nodes.statement_short: The structured moduli orbifold has a quotient-regular orbicell decomposition whose cell category is $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-$\operatorname{Graph}$.
nodes.label: thm:decomp

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.25
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis: oriented case via Harer's triangulation and ribbon graphs, unoriented via Möbius graphs. The general case pulls back along the forgetful covering and reduces to Lemma 4.26.

nodes.name: Structures on spanning graphs equal structures on surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $(S,M)$ be a stable marked surface and $\Gamma$ be a spanning graph for $(S,M)$. Then the functor \[ q_\Gamma: \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ) )\to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}\operatorname{Str}(\Gamma) \] is an equivalence of categories.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces
nodes.statement_short: Restriction to a spanning graph is an equivalence from $\mathbb{G}$-structures on the surface to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structures on the graph.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.26
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces
nodes.statement_short: Essential surjectivity by extending structured circle bundles from the graph; full faithfulness by comparing automorphism sheaves with $\underline K^{\operatorname{or}}$.

nodes.name: Object of K-membranes
nodes.statement: We introduce the notation $(K,X) := \Upsilon_* X (K)$ and refer to it as the {\em object of $K$-membranes in $X$}.

nodes.name: Derived object of K-membranes
nodes.statement: We call $(K,X)_R := R \Upsilon_* X(K)$ the {\em derived object of $K$-membranes in $X$}.

nodes.name: Subdivided interval I[n]
nodes.statement: For $n \ge 1$, we denote by $I[n] \subset \Delta^n$ the simplicial subset corresponding to the subdivided interval \[ \begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,scale=1.5] \begin{scope}[ >=stealth] \coordinate (A0) at (0,0); \coordinate (A1) at (1,0); \coordinate (B1) at (2,0); \coordinate (DOTS) at (2.5,0); \coordinate (A2) at (3,0); \coordinate (A3) at (4,0); \begin{scope}[decoration={ markings, mark=at position 0.55 with {\arrow{>}}} ] \draw[postaction={decorate}] (A0) -- (A1); \draw[postaction={decorate}] (A1) -- (B1); \draw[postaction={decorate}] (A2) -- (A3); \end{scope} {\scriptsize \draw (A0) node[anchor=south] {$0$}; \draw (A1) node[anchor=south] {$1$}; \draw (B1) node[anchor=south] {$2$}; \draw (DOTS) node {$\cdots$}; \draw (A2) node[anchor=south] {$n-1$}; \draw (A3) node[anchor=south] {$n$}; } \fill (A0) circle[radius=1pt]; \fill (A1) circle[radius=1pt]; \fill (B1) circle[radius=1pt]; \fill (A2) circle[radius=1pt]; \fill (A3) circle[radius=1pt]; \end{scope} \end{tikzpicture} \] which can be more formally described as the pushout of simplicial sets \[ \textstyle \Delta^1 \coprod_{\Delta^0} \Delta^1 \coprod_{\Delta^0} \dots \coprod_{\Delta^0} \Delta^1. \]

nodes.name: Simplicial subset of a polygon triangulation
nodes.statement: Let $P_{n+1}$ be a convex plane $(n+1)$-gon with the set of vertices labelled counterclockwise by $M = \{0,1,\cdots , n\}$. Let $\mathcal{T}$ be any triangulation of $P_{n+1}$ with vertex set $M$. A geometric triangle $\sigma$ of $\mathcal{T}$ with vertices $i,j,k$ gives rise to a unique full simplicial subset $\Delta^2 \subset \Delta^n$ with vertices $\{i\}, \{j\},\{k\}$. The union, or more formally the pushout, of the simplicial subsets of $\Delta^n$ corresponding to all triangles of $\mathcal{T}$ defines a simplicial subset $\Delta^\mathcal{T} \subset \Delta^n$ whose geometric realization is homeomorphic to $P_{n+1}$. nodes.name: 1-Segal and 2-Segal simplicial objects
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{C}$ be a combinatorial model category, and let $X \in \mathbf{C}_\Delta$ be a simplicial object. \begin{enumerate} \item We say that $X$ is {\em 1-Segal} if, for every $n\geq 1$, the morphism \[ f_n: X_n \longrightarrow (I[n], X)_R = X_1\times^R_{X_0} X_1 \times^R_{X_0} \cdots \times^R_{X_0} X_1, \] induced by the embedding $I[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta^n$, is a weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. \item We say that $X$ is {\em 2-Segal} if, for every $n\geq 2$ and every triangulation $\mathcal{T}$ of $P_{n+1}$, the morphism \[ f_\mathcal{T}: X_n \longrightarrow (\Delta^\mathcal{T}, X)_R, \] induced by the embedding $\Delta^\mathcal{T}\hookrightarrow \Delta^n$, is a weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Dyckerhoff-Kapranov, Higher Segal spaces I; Rezk 2001
nodes.label: def:segal

nodes.name: Segal conditions in a trivial model structure
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{C}$ be an ordinary category with limits and colimits. We can equip $\mathbf{C}$ with the trivial model structure such that the weak equivalences are given by the class of isomorphisms. The above Segal conditions then involve underived membrane spaces require the corresponding morphisms $f_n$, respectively $f_{\mathcal{T}}$, to be isomorphisms in $\mathbf{C}$.

nodes.name: Delta-G-set realization of a structured graph
nodes.statement: Given a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph $\Gamma$, the limit of the associated diagram $I(\Gamma) \to ({\mathcal Set}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}})^{{\operatorname{op}}}$, denoted by ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$, is called the {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set realization of $\Gamma$}.

nodes.name: Functoriality of Delta-G-set realization
nodes.statement: The ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set realization extends to a functor \[ {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \longrightarrow ({\mathcal Set}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}})^{{\operatorname{op}}}. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.6
nodes.statement: A morphism $\varphi$ between ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ consists of a functor $\varphi: I(\Gamma) \to I(\Gamma')$ of incidence categories together with a natural transformation $\eta: \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \circ \varphi \to \widetilde{I}_\Gamma$. We obtain a canonical sequence of morphisms \[ \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \longrightarrow \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \varphi \overset{\eta}{\longrightarrow} \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma} \] whose composite defines the desired morphism ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma'} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$. Here the first morphism is the natural morphism $\lim F \to \lim F \varphi$ which exists for any functor $F: I(\Gamma') \to \mathbf{C}$ provided that both limits exist. It is straightforward to verify the functoriality of this association.
nodes.statement_short: Morphisms of structured graphs induce maps of limits.

nodes.name: Structured surface invariant X(S,M)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{C}$ be a combinatorial model category, and let $X: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \to \mathbf{C}$ a ${\mathcal G}$-structured $2$-Segal object in $\mathbf{C}$. We form the right homotopy Kan extension of $X$ along the Yoneda embedding $\Upsilon: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \to ({\mathcal Set}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}})^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ and take the composite with the above functors to obtain a canonical functor \begin{equation} RX: P(S,M) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ho}(\mathbf{C}),\; \Gamma \mapsto RX({\Gamma}) \end{equation} where $RX(\Gamma) := R \Upsilon_*X ({\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma})$ and $\Gamma$ is equipped with its natural ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured from Proposition \ref{prop:emb-graph-str}. Finally, we define \[ X(S,M) := \varinjlim{} RX. \]
nodes.statement_short: Right homotopy Kan extend $X$ along Yoneda, evaluate on $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-set realizations of spanning graphs, and take the colimit over $P(S,M)$.

nodes.name: Functor RX on spanning graphs
nodes.statement: RX: P(S,M) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ho}(\mathbf{C}),\; \Gamma \mapsto RX({\Gamma})
nodes.label: eq:RX

nodes.name: Categorified state sum
nodes.statement: The object $X(S,M)$ comes equipped with a canonical isomorphism \begin{equation} RX({\Gamma}) \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} X(S,M), \end{equation} for every object $\Gamma$ in $P(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: For a 2-Segal $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-object $X$, every spanning graph computes the invariant $X(S,M)$ up to canonical isomorphism.
nodes.label: thm:state-sum

nodes.name: State sum isomorphism
nodes.statement: RX({\Gamma}) \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} X(S,M),
nodes.label: eq:statesum

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.7
nodes.statement: The claimed isomorphisms are simply the maps which consitute the colimit cone under the diagram $RX$. These maps are isomorphisms since, by Theorem \ref{thm:contractible}, the diagram $RX$ is indexed by a simply connected index category and, due to the $2$-Segal property satisfied by $X$, maps all morphisms to isomorphisms in $\operatorname{Ho}(\mathbf{C})$ (see \cite{HSS-triangulated}).
nodes.statement_short: Colimit over a simply connected index category of a diagram of isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Explicit state sum formula
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm:state-sum} shows that the structured surface invariant $X(S,M)$ can be explicitly computed via the formula \[ X(S,M) \cong \operatorname{ho}\! \underleftarrow{\lim}{}_{\{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^n \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}\}} X_n \] where $\Gamma$ is any chosen spanning graph embedded in $S$. This formula can be regarded as a categorified variant of the state sum formulas for surface invariants in the context of topological field theory.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.9
nodes.statement: Consider the functor \[ {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}, \; \Gamma \mapsto RX(\Gamma). \] Due to the $2$-Segal property of $X$, it maps weak equivalences of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs to weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. We can pass to classifying spaces to obtain a map of topological spaces. \[ |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}| \] where $W_{\mathbf{C}}$ denotes the category of weak equivalences in $\mathbf{C}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:g-graph}, we have \[ |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \simeq \coprod_{(S,M)} B\, \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) \] so that we obtain, for every stable $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface $(S,M)$, a map \[ \rho: B\, \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}|. \] The topological space $|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$ is a model for the maximal $\infty$-groupoid in the simplicial localization of $\mathbf{C}$ with respect to $W$ (cf. \cite{dwyer-kan}). Therefore, the map $\rho$ realizes a coherent action of the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ on $\rho(*) \cong X(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass $RX$ to classifying spaces of weak equivalences and use Theorem 4.12 to get $B\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)\to|W_\mathbf{C}|$.

nodes.name: Mapping class group action on structured surface invariants
nodes.statement: The structured mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ acts coherently on the object $X(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ acts coherently on $X(S,M)$.
nodes.label: thm:mod-act

nodes.name: 2-coSegal cosimplicial object
nodes.statement: We say that $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal if $\mathscr{F}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ is $2$-Segal and translate all other concepts in a similar way.

nodes.name: Fundamental groupoid relative to marked points
nodes.statement: Given a marked unoriented surface $(S,M)$, we define the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ to be the groupoid with set of objects $M$ and morphisms given by homotopy classes of paths in $S$ between points in $M$.

nodes.name: Codihedral fundamental groupoid functor
nodes.statement: Consider the codihedral groupoid \[ \mathscr{F}: \Xi \longrightarrow {\bf Grpds}, \; [n] \mapsto \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots,n\}) \] where $\Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\})$ denotes the fundamental groupoid of the unit disk $D$ in $\mathbb{C}$, relative to the subset $\{0,1,\dots,n\} \subset D$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity.

nodes.name: Codihedral fundamental groupoid is 2-coSegal
nodes.statement: The codihedral groupoid $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal. The value $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ of $\mathscr{F}$ on an unoriented marked surface $(S,M)$ is the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ of $S$ relative to $M$.
nodes.statement_short: The codihedral groupoid is 2-coSegal and its surface invariant is the fundamental groupoid relative to $M$.
nodes.label: prop:kampen

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.10
nodes.statement: To verify the $2$-Segal property, we have to show that, for any subdivision of the $n+1$-gon $P_n$ into two polygons $P_m$ with vertices $\{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}$ and $P_l$ with vertices $\{i,i+1,\dots, j\}$, the corresponding functor \[ f: \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}) \coprod_{\Pi_1(D, \{i,j\})} \Pi_1(D, \{i,i+1,\dots, j\}) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\}) \] is an isomorphism of groupoids. Up to isomorphism of groupoids we can alternatively describe $f$ as the natural functor \[ f': \Pi_1(P_m) \coprod_{\Pi_1(P_1)} \Pi_1(P_l) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(P_n) \] induced from expressing $P_n$ as the union of $P_m$ and $P_l$ with intersection $P_m \cap P_l = P_1$. Here, all fundamental groupoids are taken with respect to the vertices of the respective polygon. The fact that $f'$ is an isomorphism of groupoids is an easy instance of van Kampen's theorem (see, e.g., \cite[6.7.2]{brown}). Similarly, to compute $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$, note that we can pass to the dual of a spanning graph in $S \setminus M$ to express $(S,M)$ as a union of polygons. Interpreting formula \eqref{eq:statesum} in these terms, another application of van Kampen's theorem shows that $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ is the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ computed as a colimit parametrized by the above polygonal subdivision of $(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Van Kampen's theorem applied to polygon subdivisions.

nodes.name: Abelian groups F_n (relative homology of the disk)
nodes.statement: For $n \ge 0$, we define the abelian group $\mathscr{F}_n$ to be the kernel of the homomorphism \[ \mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{Z},\; (z_0,z_1,\dots,z_n) \mapsto \sum z_i. \]

nodes.name: Codihedral relative homology is 2-coSegal
nodes.statement: The codihedral abelian group $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal. The value $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ of $\mathscr{F}$ on an unoriented marked surface $(S,M)$ is the relative homology $H_1(S,M)$ of $S$ relative to $M$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.11
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathscr{F}_n$ can be intepreted as the relative homology of the pair $(D,\{0,1,\dots,\})$ from \S \ref{sec:fundamental}. The argument is now very similar to the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:kampen}, using the Mayer-Vietoris sequence instead of van Kampen's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: As for Proposition 5.10 with Mayer-Vietoris instead of van Kampen.

nodes.name: Topological coFukaya category
nodes.statement: The value of $\mathscr{F}$ on an oriented marked surface $(S,M)$ is called the topological coFukaya category of $(S,M)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyckerhoff-Kapranov, Triangulated surfaces in triangulated categories

nodes.name: Structured nerve cosimplicial object is 2-coSegal
nodes.statement: The ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-object $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal.

nodes.name: Intrinsic interpretation of the structured nerve invariant
nodes.statement: The question of finding a general intrinsic interpretation of $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ in terms of the $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface is open.

nodes.name: Tessellation of a convex polygon
nodes.statement: A {\em tessellation} of $P$ is a (possibly empty) set of non-intersecting diagonals in $P$.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Stasheff polytope
nodes.statement: As well known, there is a convex polytope ${\mathbb{T}}(P)$ canonically associated to $P$ and called the {\em Stasheff polytope} of $P$.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Curvilinear polygon
nodes.statement: More generally, by a {\em (curvilinear) polygon} we will mean a stable marked surface $(S,M)$ such that $S$ is, topologically, a disk and $M\subset\partial S$.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Arc on a marked surface
nodes.statement: Let now $(S,M)$ be an arbitrary stable marked surface. Following \cite{harer, fomin-shapiro-thurston}, we call an {\em arc} on $(S,M)$ an isotopy class of unoriented paths $\gamma$ beginning and ending on $M$ (possibly at the same point) such that: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] $\gamma$ does not meet any elements of $M$ other than containing them as endpoints. \item[(2)] $\gamma$ does not have any self-intersection points except possibly endpoints which coincide. \item[(3)] $\gamma$ is not homotopic (rel. endpoints) to a point, nor to a boundary segment between two adjacent marked points. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Set of arcs A(S,M)
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$ the set of arcs for $(S,M)$.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Sub-tessellation (arc system)
nodes.statement: A {\em sub-tesselation} (or an {\em arc system}) of $(S,M)$ is a finite subset $\mathcal{P}\subset \mathcal{A}(S,M)$ which can be represented by a system of pairwise non-intersecting paths.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Tessellation of a marked surface and its Stasheff polytope
nodes.statement: A {\em tessellation} of $(S,M)$ is a sub-tesselation $\mathcal{P}$ such that each $(S'_i, M'_i)\in\mathcal{P}$ is a polygon. For a tesselation $\mathcal{P}$ we define its Stasheff polytope as the product \[ {\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P}) \,\,=\,\, \prod_{(S', M')\in\mathcal{P}} {\mathbb{T}}(S', M'). \]
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Poset Tess(S,M) of tessellations
nodes.statement: The set $\operatorname{Tess}(S,M)$ of tesselations of $(S,M)$ is partially ordered by inclusion of subsets in $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Triangulation of a marked surface
nodes.statement: Maximal elements are {\em triangulations} of $(S,M)$: tesselations for which each $(S',M')$ is a triangle, i.e., $|M'|=3$, $M'\subset\partial S'$.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Tessellation complex
nodes.statement: The {\em tessellation complex} ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is a polyhedral complex obtained by gluing the polytopes ${\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P})$ for all $\mathcal{P}\in\operatorname{Tess}(S,M)$ using the face embeddings ${\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P}')\hookrightarrow {\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P})$ for $\mathcal{P}\leq\mathcal{P}'$>
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Dual graph of a tessellation
nodes.statement: Given a tessellation $\mathcal{P}\in\operatorname{Tess}(S,M)$, we associate to it its {\em dual graph} $\Gamma_\mathcal{P}$ by putting one vertex $v_{S',M'}$ inside each polygon $(S',M')\in\mathcal{P}$ and connected the adjacent $v_{(S',M')}$ be edges, similarly to \cite[\S 3.3.3]{HSS-triangulated}.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.3
nodes.statement: When $\mathcal{P}$ varies, the $\Gamma_\mathcal{P}$ run over all isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$. This implies the following.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex
nodes.statement_short: Dual graphs of tessellations run over all isotopy classes of spanning graphs.

nodes.name: Tessellation complex vs nerve of spanning graphs
nodes.statement: ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the category $P(S,M)$. \qed
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex
nodes.label: prop:tess-graph

nodes.name: Contractibility of the tessellation complex
nodes.statement: For any stable marked surface $(S,M)$ (orientable or not) the tessellation complex ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is contractible.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex
nodes.statement_short: The tessellation complex of any stable marked surface, orientable or not, is contractible.
nodes.label: thm:contractible

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A.4 (outline)
nodes.statement: Similarly to the oriented case, the proof can be extracted from the results of Harer \cite{harer}, suitably adjusted, as we now explain.
nodes.section: A.1 The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex
nodes.statement_short: Adapt Harer's argument; carried out in A.2-A.3.

nodes.name: Simplicial complex
nodes.statement: By a {\em (regular) simplicial complex} we will mean a datum $A=(V,\Sigma)$ where $V$ is a set whose elements are called {\em vertices} of $A$, and $\Sigma\subset 2^V$ is a family of finite subsets called {\em simplices} of $A$. It is required that: \begin{itemize} \item All 1-element subsets of $V$ are in $\Sigma$. \item If $I\in \Sigma$ and $I'\subset I$, then $I'\in\Sigma$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Realization of a simplicial complex
nodes.statement: The {\em realization} $|A|$ of a simplicial complex $X$ is obtained in a standard way by gluing the geometric simplices $\Delta^I$ associated to $I\in\Sigma$. Explicitly, \[ \Delta^I \,\,=\,\,\left\{ (p_a)_{a\in I}\in\mathbb{R}^I \bigl| \,\, p_a\geq 0, \,\,\sum_{a\in I} p_a =1\right\}. \]
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Simplicial subcomplex
nodes.statement: A {\em simplicial subcomplex} of $A=(V,\Sigma)$ is a simplicial complex $A'=(V',\Sigma')$ s.t. $V'\subset V$ and $\Sigma'\subset\Sigma$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Classical and monotone nerves of coverings
nodes.statement: (a) Let $X$ be a space and $\mathcal{U} = (U_a)_{a\in V}$ be a locally finite covering of $X$ by closed subspaces $U_a$. The {\em classical nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{N}\mathcal{U}=(V, \Sigma)$ where $\Sigma$ consists of finite $I\subset V$ s.t. $\bigcap_{v\in I} U_v\neq\emptyset$. \vskip .2cm (b) In the situation (a), assume that the covering $\mathcal{U}$ is {\em saturated}, i.e., for any $U,U'\in \mathcal{U}$ the intersection $U\cap U'$ is either empty or belongs to $\mathcal{U}$. The {\em monotone nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U} = (V.\Sigma^\leq)$, where $\Sigma^\leq$ consists of $I=\{v_0, \cdots, v_p\}\subset V$ such that $U_{v_{s(0)}}\subset U_{v_{s(1)}} \subset \cdots\subset U_{v_{s(p)}}$ for some permutation $s$ of $\{0,1,\cdots, p\}$. Thus $|\operatorname{N}^\leq(\mathcal{U})|$ is the geometric realization of the simplicial set, given by the nerve of the poset of nonempty $U\in\mathcal{U}$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Classical nerve of a covering
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a space and $\mathcal{U} = (U_a)_{a\in V}$ be a locally finite covering of $X$ by closed subspaces $U_a$. The {\em classical nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{N}\mathcal{U}=(V, \Sigma)$ where $\Sigma$ consists of finite $I\subset V$ s.t. $\bigcap_{v\in I} U_v\neq\emptyset$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Saturated covering and monotone nerve
nodes.statement: In the situation (a), assume that the covering $\mathcal{U}$ is {\em saturated}, i.e., for any $U,U'\in \mathcal{U}$ the intersection $U\cap U'$ is either empty or belongs to $\mathcal{U}$. The {\em monotone nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U} = (V.\Sigma^\leq)$, where $\Sigma^\leq$ consists of $I=\{v_0, \cdots, v_p\}\subset V$ such that $U_{v_{s(0)}}\subset U_{v_{s(1)}} \subset \cdots\subset U_{v_{s(p)}}$ for some permutation $s$ of $\{0,1,\cdots, p\}$. Thus $|\operatorname{N}^\leq(\mathcal{U})|$ is the geometric realization of the simplicial set, given by the nerve of the poset of nonempty $U\in\mathcal{U}$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Nerve theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] Assume that any finite intersection $U_{v_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{v_p}$ is either empty or contractible. Then $|\operatorname{N}\mathcal{U}|$ is homotopy equivalent to $X$. \item[(b)] If, moreover, $\mathcal{U}$ is saturated, then $|\operatorname{N}^\leq \mathcal{U}|$ is homotopy equivalent to $X$. \qed \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold
nodes.statement_short: Nerves of good (saturated) closed coverings are homotopy equivalent to the space.
nodes.label: prop:nerve-classical

nodes.name: Barycentric subdivision
nodes.statement: The {\em barycentric subdivision} of a simplicial complex $A=(V,\Sigma)$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{Bar}(A)=(V_{\operatorname{Bar}},\Sigma_{\operatorname{Bar}})$, where $V_{\operatorname{Bar}}=\Sigma$ and $\Sigma_{\operatorname{Bar}}$ consists of finite subsets $\{I_0, \cdots, I_p\}$ such that $I_{s(0)} \subset I_{s(1)} \subset \cdots\subset I_{s(p)}$ for some permutation $s$ of $\{0,1,\cdots, p\}$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Link of a simplex
nodes.statement: For each simplex $I\in\Sigma$ we have the sub complex $A_I\subset{\operatorname{Bar}}(A)$ called the {\em link} of $I$. By definition, $A_I=(V_I, \Sigma_I)$, where \[ V_I \,\,=\,\,\bigl\{ {\operatorname{bar}}(J)\bigl| \,\, J\supset I,\,\, J\in\Sigma \bigr\}, \quad \Sigma_I \,\,=\,\, \bigl\{ \{ {\operatorname{bar}}(J_0), \cdots, {\operatorname{bar}}(J_p)\}, \,\,\, I\subset J_0\subset\cdots \subset J_p\bigr\}. \]
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Dual subcomplex
nodes.statement: If $A'$ is a subcomplex of $A$ as above, we define the {\em dual subcomplex} to $(A,A')$ as \[ (A,A')^\vee \,\,=\,\,\bigcup_{I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'} A_I \,\,\,\subset \,\,\, {\operatorname{Bar}}(A). \]
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Dual subcomplex models the complement
nodes.statement: The realization $|(A,A')^\vee|$ is homotopy equivalent to $|A|-|A'|$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold
nodes.label: prop:dual-CW

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.7
nodes.statement: We consider the covering $\mathcal{U}$ of $|A|-|A'|$ by closed subsets $\Delta^I_0 = \Delta^I \cap (|A|-|A'|)$ for $I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'$. This covering is saturated, and $(A,A')^\vee=\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U}$. As each $\Delta^I_0$ is contractible, our statement follows from Proposition \ref{prop:nerve-classical}.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold
nodes.statement_short: The closed simplices cover the complement saturatedly with contractible pieces; apply the nerve theorem.

nodes.name: Triangulated manifold
nodes.statement: By a {\em triangulated manifold} we mean a pair $(A, A')$ consisting of a simplicial complex $A$ and a subcomplex $A'$ such that $|A|-|A'|$ is a topological manifold.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Dual cell
nodes.statement: In this case each $|A_I|$, $I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'$, is a topological cell which we call the {\em dual cell} to $I$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Arc complex
nodes.statement: The {\em arc complex} $A=A(S,M)$ is the simplicial complex with the set of vertices $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$ and simplices being sub-tesselations.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Subcomplex A_infinity of non-tessellations
nodes.statement: It has a subcomplex $A_\infty=A_\infty(S,M)$ formed by sub-tesselations which are not tesselations.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Tessellation complex as dual complex of the arc complex
nodes.statement: The tessellation complex ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is homeomorphic to $|(A, A_\infty)^\vee|$ so that each cell ${\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P})$ is identified with $A_\mathcal{P}$, the link of $\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.label: prop:tess-A

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.8
nodes.statement: Clear by comparing the definitions.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.statement_short: Compare definitions.

nodes.name: Harer's triangulation of Teichmuller space (unoriented case)
nodes.statement: There is a homeomorphism $\Psi=\Psi_{S,M}: |A|-|A_\infty| \to \operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$, equivariant with respect to the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.statement_short: The arc complex minus its infinity part is equivariantly homeomorphic to $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$, for orientable or not.
nodes.label: thm:harer-triang

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A.9
nodes.statement: The construction and the argument of \cite{harer} extend to the general case as follows. A point $p\in |A|-|A_\infty|$ lies, by definition, strictly inside a simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ for some tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ and thus is represented by the collection of its barycentric coordinates \[ (p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}, \,\, p_\gamma > 0,\,\, \sum p_\gamma = 1, \] one for each arc $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}$. Consider a polygon $(S'_i, M'_i)$ of $\mathcal{P}$. To each edge $e$ of $S'_i$ we associate the ``length" $p_e:=p_\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is the arc of $\mathcal{P}$ that gave rise to $e$. Let $l_e=\sum_{e\subset\partial S'_i} p_e$ be the total ``length" of $\partial S'_i$. Let $S''_i$ be a disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with center $0$ and circumference $l_e$. We can map $M'_i$ bijectively to a subset $M''_i\subset \partial S''_i$ so that the distances (on $\partial S''_i$) between neighboring elements of $M''_i$ match the corresponding numbers $p_e$ for the edges of $S'_i$. In this way we get a stable marked Klein surface $(S''_i, M''_i)$. We now glue the $(S''_i, M''_i)$ together in the same fashion as the $(S'_i, M'_i)$ are glued together to form $(S, M)$. For this, we use the identifications of the boundary arcs of different $S''_i$ which are affine linear in the standard angle (or arc length) coordinates on the circles $\partial S''_i$. In this way we get a Klein surface $(S'', M'')$, identified with $(S,M)$ by a diffeomorphism unique up to isotopy. In other words, we get a point of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$. This defines the map $\Psi_{S,M}$. Its $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-equivariance is clear. The fact that $\Psi_{S,M}$ is a homeomorphism, was proved in \cite{harer} in the oriented case. Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, and let $\varpi: (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)\to (S,M)$ be its orientation cover, with the deck involution $\tau$ preserving $\widetilde M$. By equivariance, the homeomorphism \[ \Psi_{\widetilde S, \widetilde M}: \,\, |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)| \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich} (\widetilde S, \widetilde M) \] sends the involution $\tau_A: |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\to |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|$ induced by $\tau$, to $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. Because of Proposition \ref{thm:klein-teich}(b2), we are reduced to the following. \begin{lem} We have \[ \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \,\,=\,\, |A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|. \] \end{lem} \noindent {\sl Proof of the lemma:} A point $p\in |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|^{\tau_A}$ lies in a $\tau$-invariant simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ corresponding to a $\tau$-invariant sub-tesselation $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ of $(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}$. We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$ does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering). So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation. Further, suppose that $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation, Then any polygon $(\widetilde S'_i, \widetilde M'_i)$ of $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation. We conclude that \[ p\,\,\in \,\, \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \] must lie in a simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ where $\widetilde\mathcal{P}=\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{P})$ is the preimage of a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of $(S,M)$ and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates $(p_{\widetilde\gamma})_{{\widetilde\gamma}\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ which is $\tau$-invariant. Such collections of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ in $|A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|$. This proves the lemma and Theorem \ref{thm:harer-triang}.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.statement_short: Build a Klein surface from barycentric coordinates by gluing disks with arc-length data. Reduce the unoriented case to $\tau$-fixed points via the orientation cover and Lemma A.10.

nodes.name: Fixed points of the arc complex of the orientation cover
nodes.statement: We have \[ \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \,\,=\,\, |A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|. \]
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.10
nodes.statement: A point $p\in |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|^{\tau_A}$ lies in a $\tau$-invariant simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ corresponding to a $\tau$-invariant sub-tesselation $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ of $(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}$. We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$ does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering). So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation. Further, suppose that $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation, Then any polygon $(\widetilde S'_i, \widetilde M'_i)$ of $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation. We conclude that \[ p\,\,\in \,\, \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \] must lie in a simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ where $\widetilde\mathcal{P}=\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{P})$ is the preimage of a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of $(S,M)$ and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates $(p_{\widetilde\gamma})_{{\widetilde\gamma}\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ which is $\tau$-invariant. Such collections of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ in $|A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|$. This proves the lemma and Theorem \ref{thm:harer-triang}.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.statement_short: Images of $\tau$-invariant (sub-)tessellations under the covering are (sub-)tessellations, matching barycentric coordinates.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.14
nodes.statement: Now, Propositions \ref{prop:tess-graph}, \ref{prop:tess-A} and \ref{prop:dual-CW} together with the fact that $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is homeomorphic to a Euclidean space (Theorem \ref{thm:klein-teich}(c)) imply Theorem \ref{thm:graph-contr}.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.statement_short: Combine Propositions A.3, A.7, A.8 with Euclideanity of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$.

nodes.name: Factor lambda through signed permutations
nodes.statement: Consider the functor \[ \lambda: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\mathcal Set}, \; [n] \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([0], [n])/\mathfrak{G}_0 \] from Proposition \ref{prop:forget}. We claim that $\lambda$ admits a canonical factorization over the forgetful functor ${\Delta {\mathfrak W}} \to {\mathcal Set}$. Note that, via $\lambda$, the group $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts canonically on the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([0],[n]) = \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ of vertices of the combinatorial $n$-simplex. A vertex $i \in \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ can be canonically identified with the corresponding degeneracy map \[ s_i: [n+1] \longrightarrow [n],\; j \mapsto \begin{cases} j & \text{for $j \le i$,}\\ j-1 & \text{for $j > i$.} \end{cases} \] Explicitly, given $g \in \mathfrak{G}_n$ and $i \in \{0,1,\dots,n\}$, we have a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ [n+1] \ar[d]_{s_j^*g} \ar[r]^{s_i} & [n] \ar[d]^g\\ [n+1] \ar[r]^{s_j} & [n] } \] where $j = \lambda(g)(i)$. Clearly, the map $\lambda(s_j^*g)$ induces a map from the fiber $s_i^{-1}(i) = \{i,i+1\}$ to the fiber $s_j^{-1}(j) = \{j,j+1\}$ which is either order preserving or order reversing. Therefore, we can lift $\lambda(g) \in S_{n+1}$ to a signed permutation \[ \widetilde{\lambda}(g) = (\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n ; \lambda(g)) \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \wreath S_{n+1} \] where \[ \varepsilon_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if $\lambda(s_j^*g): \{i,i+1\} \to \{j,j+1\}$ is order preserving,}\\ 1 & \text{if $\lambda(s_j^*g): \{i,i+1\} \to \{j,j+1\}$ is order reversing.} \end{cases} \] Using the unique factorization property in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$, it is straightforward to verify that the association $g \mapsto \widetilde{\lambda}(g)$ extends to provide a functor \[ \widetilde{\lambda}: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\Delta {\mathfrak W}} \] commuting with the forgetful functors to ${\mathcal Set}$, which proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $\lambda$ factors canonically through $\Delta\mathfrak{W}\to\mathcal{S}et$, proving (1).

nodes.name: Vertices as degeneracies
nodes.statement: Note that, via $\lambda$, the group $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts canonically on the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([0],[n]) = \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ of vertices of the combinatorial $n$-simplex. A vertex $i \in \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ can be canonically identified with the corresponding degeneracy map \[ s_i: [n+1] \longrightarrow [n],\; j \mapsto \begin{cases} j & \text{for $j \le i$,}\\ j-1 & \text{for $j > i$.} \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Identify vertices with degeneracy maps $s_i$.

nodes.name: Fiber map of degeneracies
nodes.statement: Explicitly, given $g \in \mathfrak{G}_n$ and $i \in \{0,1,\dots,n\}$, we have a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ [n+1] \ar[d]_{s_j^*g} \ar[r]^{s_i} & [n] \ar[d]^g\\ [n+1] \ar[r]^{s_j} & [n] } \] where $j = \lambda(g)(i)$. Clearly, the map $\lambda(s_j^*g)$ induces a map from the fiber $s_i^{-1}(i) = \{i,i+1\}$ to the fiber $s_j^{-1}(j) = \{j,j+1\}$ which is either order preserving or order reversing.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda(s_j^*g)$ maps the fiber $\{i,i+1\}$ monotonically or antitonically.

nodes.name: Signed lift
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can lift $\lambda(g) \in S_{n+1}$ to a signed permutation \[ \widetilde{\lambda}(g) = (\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n ; \lambda(g)) \in \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \wreath S_{n+1} \] where \[ \varepsilon_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if $\lambda(s_j^*g): \{i,i+1\} \to \{j,j+1\}$ is order preserving,}\\ 1 & \text{if $\lambda(s_j^*g): \{i,i+1\} \to \{j,j+1\}$ is order reversing.} \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Define the signed permutation $\widetilde\lambda(g)$ via orientation of fibers.

nodes.name: Functoriality of the lift
nodes.statement: Using the unique factorization property in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$, it is straightforward to verify that the association $g \mapsto \widetilde{\lambda}(g)$ extends to provide a functor \[ \widetilde{\lambda}: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \longrightarrow {\Delta {\mathfrak W}} \] commuting with the forgetful functors to ${\mathcal Set}$, which proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: Unique factorization makes $\widetilde\lambda$ a functor, proving (1).

nodes.name: Kernel acts trivially on faces
nodes.statement: The remaining statements are easy to verify, the only nonobvious point being that ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}'$ is in fact noncrossed simplicial. But this follows from the construction of $\widetilde{\lambda}$: For $g \in \mathfrak{G}_n$, the condition $\lambda(g) = \operatorname{id} \in S_{n+1}$ implies that $g^*$ fixes all face maps $[n-1] \to [n]$.
nodes.statement_short: Elements with $\lambda(g)=\operatorname{id}$ fix all face maps.

nodes.name: Kernel is a simplicial group
nodes.statement: The condition that all signs $\varepsilon_i$ of the lift $\widetilde{\lambda(g)}$ are $0$ implies that $g^*$ fixes all degeneracy maps $[n+1] \to [n]$. But this implies that ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}''$ is a simplicial group (cf. Example \ref{exa:deviation}).
nodes.statement_short: Trivial signs force fixing degeneracies, so the kernel is a simplicial group.

nodes.name: Semidirect product is semiconstant
nodes.statement: The semidirect product $G \ltimes \Delta$ has the unique factorization property: $(g, \phi) = (1, \phi) \circ (g, \operatorname{id})$ making it a semiconstant crossed simplicial group.
nodes.statement_short: $(g,\phi)=(1,\phi)\circ(g,\operatorname{id})$ gives unique factorization.
nodes.section: 1.3 Semiconstant crossed simplicial groups and twisted group actions

nodes.name: Semiconstant is semidirect
nodes.statement: Given a semiconstant crossed simplicial group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$, it follows from \eqref{eq:semiconstant} that $\mathfrak{G}_0$ acts on $\Delta$. It immediately follows from the definition that we may identify ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ with $\mathfrak{G}_0 \ltimes \Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: The square (1.3.1) gives a $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action on $\Delta$ identifying $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ with $\mathfrak{G}_0\ltimes\Delta$.
nodes.section: 1.3 Semiconstant crossed simplicial groups and twisted group actions

nodes.name: Part (a) and identification of |G|
nodes.statement: (a) was shown by Fiedorowicz and Loday \cite{fiedorowicz-loday}. The identification of $|\mathfrak{G}|$ in the examples of (b) is also immediate from their considerations.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Fiedorowicz-Loday for (a) and the identification in (b).

nodes.name: Cyclic, paracyclic, dihedral, quaternionic cases
nodes.statement: The remaining parts are well known \cite{DHK} \cite[Ch.7]{loday} in the cyclic and paracyclic cases $\Delta \mathfrak{G}=\Lambda, \Lambda_\infty$, and were extended by Dunn \cite{dunn} to the dihedral and quaternionic cases.
nodes.statement_short: Known results of Dwyer-Hopkins-Kan, Loday and Dunn.

nodes.name: Subdivided cases
nodes.statement: The $N$-subdivided cases can be deduced from these using the fact that $\operatorname{sd}_N^*$ does not change the geometric realization.
nodes.statement_short: Edgewise subdivision preserves geometric realization.

nodes.name: Paradihedral case
nodes.statement: The paradihedral case can be deduced from the paracyclic one by identifying $\Xi_\infty$ with the semi-direct product of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\Lambda_\infty$. We leave the remaining details to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\Xi_\infty$ as a semidirect product of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\Lambda_\infty$.

nodes.name: Recall G = |G|
nodes.statement: We recall that $G$ is identified with $|\mathfrak{G}|$ by Theorem \ref{thm:crossed-groups}(b1).
nodes.statement_short: Use Theorem 1.33(b1).

nodes.name: Embedding epsilon
nodes.statement: A homomorphism $\epsilon: \mathfrak{G}_0\to |\mathfrak{G}|$ is obtained from the compatible system of homomorphisms $\omega_n^*: \mathfrak{G}_0\to \mathfrak{G}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\epsilon$ from the maps $\omega_n^*$.

nodes.name: Case by case verification
nodes.statement: The verification that $\epsilon$ is an embedding with the required properties, is obtained using case by case analysis.
nodes.statement_short: Check the required properties case by case.

nodes.name: Simplicial structure
nodes.statement: The cosimplicial structure is obtained by letting face maps act by insertion of $1$ and degeneracy maps act by multiplication in $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Faces insert units, degeneracies multiply.

nodes.name: Wreath product
nodes.statement: Let us construct an action of $\mathfrak{G}_n$ on $A^{\otimes (n+1)}$. Consider the wreath product \[ S_{n+1}\wr \mathfrak{G}_0 := S_{n+1}\ltimes \mathfrak{G}_0^{n+1}, \] where the action of $S_{n+1}$ on $\mathfrak{G}_0^{n+1}$ is by permuting the Cartesian factors. Note that we have a projection map $S_{n+1}\wr\mathfrak{G}_0 \to S_{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $S_{n+1}\wr\mathfrak{G}_0$ with its projection to $S_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Lift L_n of lambda_n
nodes.statement: We now claim that the homomorphism $\lambda_n: \mathfrak{G}_n\to S_{n+1}$ from Proposition \ref{prop:forget} has a natural lifting to a homomorphism \[ L_n: \mathfrak{G}_n \longrightarrow S_{n+1}\wr \mathfrak{G}_0. \] Indeed, by the canonical factorization \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n]) = \mathfrak{G}_0 \times\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n]), \] and $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts on this set on the left by composition of morphisms in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$. We see, first, that the action of any $g\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ takes any fiber of the projection to $\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n])$ to another fiber. The induced permutation of these fibers is precisely $\lambda_n(g)\in S_{n+1}$. Second, if we identify each fiber with $\mathfrak{G}_0$, then the identification of one fiber with another is given by the left multiplication with some element of $\mathfrak{G}_0$, These elements, together with $\lambda_n(g)$, give the desired $L_n(g)\in S_{n+1}\wr \mathfrak{G}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $\lambda_n$ to $L_n:\mathfrak{G}_n\to S_{n+1}\wr\mathfrak{G}_0$ using the fibers of $\operatorname{Hom}([0],[n])$.

nodes.name: Pull back the action
nodes.statement: Since $\mathfrak{G}_0$ acts on $A$ as a vector space, we have the natural action of $S_{n+1}\wr\mathfrak{G}_0$ on $A^{\otimes(n+1)}$ which combines the permutations of the tensor factors and action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ on each factor. We pull this action back along $L_n$ to get a $\mathfrak{G}_n$-action on $A^{\otimes(n+1)}$. The compatibility of these actions with the simplicial structure is verified straightforwardly.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back the natural wreath action on $A^{\otimes(n+1)}$ along $L_n$.

nodes.name: Define psi_*
nodes.statement: Let $\psi=(\psi_{f,f'})$ be a morphism from $(I', \mathcal{O}(I'))$ to $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ in $\mathcal{G}$. The map $\psi_*: I'\to I$ is defined to be the value, on $\psi$, of the functor $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi_*$ is the value of $\lambda_\mathcal{G}$.

nodes.name: Define psi^*
nodes.statement: To define the map $\psi^*: \mathcal{O}(I)\to\mathcal{O}(I')$ associated to $\psi$, we fix $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$, choose and arbitrary $f'\in\mathcal{O}(I')$ and interpret them as vertical isomorphisms in the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ (I', \mathcal{O}(I')) \ar[rr]^\psi && (I, \mathcal{O}(I)) \\ \epsilon[n'] \ar[u]^{f'} \ar[rr]^{\psi_{f, f'} = f^{-1}\circ\psi\circ f' }&& \epsilon[n] \ar[u]_f \\\epsilon[n']\ar[u]^{g'} \ar[urr]_\phi } \] Next, we define $\phi$ and $g'$ in the diagram via the canonical factorization $\psi_{f, f'} = \phi\circ g'$ with $\phi\in\Delta$, $g'\in\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$, and set $\psi^*(f)=f'\circ g'$. The result is independent of $f'$ in virtue of the equivariance condition on the datum $\psi=(\psi_{f, f'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Canonical factorization $\psi_{f,f'}=\phi\circ g'$ and $\psi^*(f)=f'\circ g'$.

nodes.name: Pair defined
nodes.statement: This defines the pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ associated to $\psi$. We leave the remaining verifications to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining verifications left to the reader.

nodes.name: Use linear-order model
nodes.statement: We use the model of $\mathcal{G}/I$ from Proposition \ref{prop:model-G/I}.
nodes.statement_short: Work with the model of Proposition 2.8.

nodes.name: Restriction on objects
nodes.statement: Given a total order $\leq $ on $I$, it restricts to a total order on $I'$, and so we have a diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\sigma'} \ar[r]^\phi& \{0,1, \dots, n\}\ar[d]^\sigma \\ I'\ar[r]_u& I, } \end{equation} in which $\psi, u$ are monotone embeddings, and $\sigma,\sigma'$ are monotone bijections. We define on objects $\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)=(I', \mathcal{O}_{\sigma'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict total orders and set $\operatorname{Res}(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)=(I',\mathcal{O}_{\sigma'})$.

nodes.name: Two orders and their restrictions
nodes.statement:
Further, let $g\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ be such that $\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2$, where $\sigma_1, \sigma_2: \{0,1, \dots, n\}	o I$ are the bijections corresponding to two total orders $\leq^1, \leq^2$ on $I$. Let $\sigma'_1, \sigma'_2: \{0,1,\dots, n'\}	o I'$ be the bijections corresponding to the restrictions of $\leq^1, \leq^2$ to $I'$. We the have two commutative diagrams as in \eqref{eq:comm-diagr-emb}, whose arrows we denote $u, \sigma'_
u, \sigma_
u, \phi_
u$, $
u=1,2$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up diagrams for two orders related by $g$.

nodes.name: Claim phi_2 = g^* phi_1
nodes.statement: We claim, first of all, that $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$. Indeed, consider the canonical diagram in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ \[ \xymatrix{ [n']\ar[d]_{\phi_1^*g} \ar[r]^{g^*\phi_1}&[n] \ar[d]^g \\ [n']\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& [n] } \] defining $g^*\phi_1$ and apply the functor $\lambda$ to it. Because of the assumptions on $g$, the resulting diagram in ${\bf FSet}$ is \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)} \ar[r]^{\phi_2}& \{0,1,\dots, n\} \ar[d]^{\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma^2} \\ \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& \{0,1,\dots, n\}, } \end{equation} whence $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.

nodes.name: Canonical square
nodes.statement: Indeed, consider the canonical diagram in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ \[ \xymatrix{ [n']\ar[d]_{\phi_1^*g} \ar[r]^{g^*\phi_1}&[n] \ar[d]^g \\ [n']\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& [n] } \] defining $g^*\phi_1$ and apply the functor $\lambda$ to it.
nodes.statement_short: Consider the canonical square defining $g^*\phi_1$ and apply $\lambda$.
