nodes.name: Read off phi_2
nodes.statement: Because of the assumptions on $g$, the resulting diagram in ${\bf FSet}$ is \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)} \ar[r]^{\phi_2}& \{0,1,\dots, n\} \ar[d]^{\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma^2} \\ \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& \{0,1,\dots, n\}, } \end{equation} whence $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.
nodes.statement_short: The image diagram gives $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.

nodes.name: Restricted permutation
nodes.statement: We further claim that $\lambda_n(\phi_1^*(g)) = (\sigma'_1)^{-1}\sigma'_2$. Indeed, in virtue of the injectivity of $\phi_1, \phi_2$ and bijectivity of $\lambda_n(g)$, there can be at most one map making \eqref{eq:2.1.11} commutative, and both sides of the proposed equality do.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)=(\sigma_1')^{-1}\sigma_2'$ by uniqueness.

nodes.name: Restriction on morphisms
nodes.statement: So we define $\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}$ on morphisms by sending $g$ to $\phi_1^*(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: Send $g$ to $\phi_1^*(g)$.

nodes.name: Functoriality
nodes.statement_short: Use the first crossed identity of Proposition 1.2(c).

nodes.name: Claim: pi_0 extends to an equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $(C,J)$ be a marked $G$-structured circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure group along $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. We claim that the association \[ (C,J) \mapsto (\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)}), \] where $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ denotes the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set constructed in Lemma \ref{lem:pi0} below, extends to an equivalence of categories $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$. Given a morphism $(\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi}): (C,J) \to (C', J')$ of marked $G$-structured circles, we have to construct a morphism of the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ and $(\pi_0(J'),\rho_{\pi_0(J')})$. Clearly, we have an induced map $\psi: \pi_0(J) \to \pi_0(J')$ of underlying sets. We now define the pullback map $\psi^*: \pi_0(F_{J'}) \to \pi_0(F_{J})$ of structured frames. Let $f \in F_{J'}$ represent a structured frame in $\pi_0(F_{J'})$. Its image under $\rho$ defines a homeomorphism $\rho(f): { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C')$ which maps $[n]$ to $J'$. We choose a point in the unique component of $C'\setminus J'$ bounded by $\rho(f)(n)$ and $\rho(f)(0)$, and denote its preimage in $C$ under $\varphi$ by $p$. Note that $p$ lies in $C \setminus J$. Consider the homeomorphism $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$ in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$. Now we choose a path $\alpha: [0,1] \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ starting at $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$, ending at a homeomorphism which maps $[m]$ to $J$, such that, for all $t \in [0,1]$, $\alpha(t)(0) \ne p$. It is easy to see that the space of such paths is contractible. Since $F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ is a covering, there is a unique lift of $\alpha$ to $F$ satisfying $\alpha(0) = \widetilde{\varphi}$. We define $\psi^*(f)$ to be the connected component of $\alpha(1)$ in the space $F_J$. The pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ defines a morphism in $\mathcal{G}$ by Proposition \ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}. It straightforward to show that this construction is functorial.
nodes.statement_short: The association $(C,J)\mapsto(\pi_0(J),\rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ extends to a functor.

nodes.name: Induced map of underlying sets
nodes.statement: Given a morphism $(\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi}): (C,J) \to (C', J')$ of marked $G$-structured circles, we have to construct a morphism of the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ and $(\pi_0(J'),\rho_{\pi_0(J')})$. Clearly, we have an induced map $\psi: \pi_0(J) \to \pi_0(J')$ of underlying sets.
nodes.statement_short: A morphism induces $\psi:\pi_0(J)\to\pi_0(J')$.

nodes.name: Choose base point p
nodes.statement: We now define the pullback map $\psi^*: \pi_0(F_{J'}) \to \pi_0(F_{J})$ of structured frames. Let $f \in F_{J'}$ represent a structured frame in $\pi_0(F_{J'})$. Its image under $\rho$ defines a homeomorphism $\rho(f): { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C')$ which maps $[n]$ to $J'$. We choose a point in the unique component of $C'\setminus J'$ bounded by $\rho(f)(n)$ and $\rho(f)(0)$, and denote its preimage in $C$ under $\varphi$ by $p$. Note that $p$ lies in $C \setminus J$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a frame $f$ and a point $p$ in the gap between $\rho(f)(n)$ and $\rho(f)(0)$.

nodes.name: Path avoiding p
nodes.statement: Consider the homeomorphism $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$ in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$. Now we choose a path $\alpha: [0,1] \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ starting at $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$, ending at a homeomorphism which maps $[m]$ to $J$, such that, for all $t \in [0,1]$, $\alpha(t)(0) \ne p$. It is easy to see that the space of such paths is contractible.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a path of homeomorphisms avoiding $p$; the space of such paths is contractible.

nodes.name: Lift and define psi^*
nodes.statement: Since $F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ is a covering, there is a unique lift of $\alpha$ to $F$ satisfying $\alpha(0) = \widetilde{\varphi}$. We define $\psi^*(f)$ to be the connected component of $\alpha(1)$ in the space $F_J$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the path to $F$ and set $\psi^*(f)$ to the component of the endpoint.

nodes.name: Morphism and functoriality
nodes.statement: The pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ defines a morphism in $\mathcal{G}$ by Proposition \ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}. It straightforward to show that this construction is functorial.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.6 gives a morphism; the construction is functorial.

nodes.name: Equivalence
nodes.statement: To see that it provides an equivalence of categories it suffices to verify the unique factorization property for the full subcategory of ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ generated by a set of standard objects $\{ (S^1, [n]) \}$ which is easily done.
nodes.statement_short: Check unique factorization on standard objects.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: (1) As argued in Proposition \ref{prop:homeo-contr}, each component of the subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n])$ is contractible. Therefore, the map $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$ restricts to a covering $H_n \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1,[n])$ which is topologically trivial so that each connected component of $H_n$ must be contracible. We have \[ \pi_0 { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \cong D_{n+1} \cong \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_\Xi([n]) \] where $\Xi$ denotes the dihedral category of Example \ref {ex:dihedral}. The group $\pi_0(H_n)$ can be identified with the preimage $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})$ under $p: G\to O(2)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:crossed-groups}(b2), this preimage is canonically identified with $\mathfrak{G}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Components of $H_n$ are contractible and $\pi_0(H_n)\cong\mathfrak{G}_n$ by Theorem 1.33(b2).

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: (2) Passing to connected components, we obtain a sequence of maps \[ \pi_0(F_J) \overset{\pi_0(\rho_J)}{\longrightarrow} \pi_0({ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J))) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}([n], \pi_0(J)) \] whose composite is defined to be $\rho_{\pi_0(J)}$. It is apparent that $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set.
nodes.statement_short: Compose induced maps on $\pi_0$ to get the structure map.

nodes.name: Drinfeld's approach
nodes.statement: The argument is similar to that of \cite{drinfeld:cyclic}. That is, let $\bf\Delta$ be the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, and ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta}\to \mathcal{G}$ be the functor of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure, extending $i$ (Example \ref{ex:DG-closure}).
nodes.statement_short: Use the $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-closure functor.

nodes.name: Drinfeld colimit formula
nodes.statement: A simplicial set $Y$ can be seen as a contravariant functor $Y: {\bf\Delta}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and, as pointed out in Formula (1.1) of \cite {drinfeld:cyclic}, \[ |Y|\,\,=\,\,\varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, Y\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr), \] where $F$ runs over finite subsets of $[0,1]$, and $\pi_0([0,1]-F)$ is equipped by the total order induced by that on $[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: $|Y|$ as a colimit over finite subsets of $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Rewrite over the circle
nodes.statement: Now, if $X$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set, we can view $X$ as a contravariant functor $\mathcal{G}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and identify \[ \begin{gathered} |i^*X| \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, ({\bf i}^*X)\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr) \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0([0,1]-F))\bigr) \,\,= \\ =\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{1\in F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr) \,\,=\,\, \,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr). \end{gathered} \] Here we view $S^1$ as obtained from $[0,1]$ by identifying $0$ and $1$ into one point $1\in S^1$ and as equipped with the standard ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a colimit over finite subsets of $S^1$.

nodes.name: Action
nodes.statement: Each set $\pi_0(S^1-F)$ is then equipped with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure by Corollary \ref{cor:structured-circle-orders}. Now, the last colimit is manifestly acted upon by ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 2.15 structures the index sets; $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$ acts.

nodes.name: Complement duality on C_G
nodes.statement: We define the functor $(-)^{\vee}: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to { {\EuScript C}_G}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ by putting \[ (C,J)^{\vee} := (C, \overline{C \setminus J}), \quad (\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi})^{\vee} := (\varphi^{-1}, \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1}) \] on objects and morphisms, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Define $(C,J)^\vee=(C,\overline{C\setminus J})$.

nodes.name: Involution is an equivalence
nodes.statement: Since the square of this functor equals the identity functor, it must be an equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: The functor squares to the identity.

nodes.name: Transport to Delta-G
nodes.statement: Further, since ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is equivalent to ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$, we conclude that there exists a duality functor $(-)^\vee_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \overset{\simeq}{\to} {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\operatorname{op}}$ with $[n]^\vee=[n]$. The choice of values for this functor on morphisms, however, is not canonical.
nodes.statement_short: Transport via $\Delta\mathfrak{G}\simeq\mathcal{C}_G$.

nodes.name: Self-contained proof
nodes.statement: Although this is a particular case of the general duality for planar crossed simplicial groups, let us provide a self-contained proof for convenience of the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Give a direct proof.

nodes.name: Dual map of refinements
nodes.statement: Given a morphism of cyclically ordered sets $f: J \to K$, we obtain a map of sets of linear refinements $f^{\vee}: K^{\vee} \to J^{\vee}$. To lift this map to a morphism of cyclically ordered sets, we have to additionally provide a linear order on each fiber of $f^{\vee}$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ induces $f^\vee$ on linear refinements; need fiber orders.

nodes.name: Order on fibers
nodes.statement: Consider linear orders $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \in K^{\vee}$ which map to the same linear order $\lambda \in J^{\vee}$. Let $j_{\max}$ be the maximum of $(J, \lambda)$. We say $\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2$ if \[ \big|\{k \in K\; |\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_1} k\}\big| \le \big|\{k \in K \;|\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_2} k\}\big|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare positions of $f(j_{\max})$ to order the fibers.

nodes.name: Compatibility
nodes.statement: This construction provides linear orders on the fibers of $f^{\vee}$ which are compatible with the cyclic order on $K^{\vee}$.
nodes.statement_short: The fiber orders are compatible with the cyclic order.

nodes.name: Double dual
nodes.statement: The equivalence of categories can be verified by noting that the double dual $(J^{\vee})^{\vee}$ can be canonically and functorially identified with $J$.
nodes.statement_short: $(J^\vee)^\vee\cong J$ functorially.

nodes.name: (ii) implies (i)
nodes.statement: Clearly, (i) implies (ii) and (iii). Let us prove that (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i). Let $J\hookrightarrow C$ be an embedding into a circle defining the dihedral order. Since $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$, we have that $x_0, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are in the right dihedral order. In other words, their embedding into a circle $C$ is such that they subdivide $C$ into the following (unoriented) arcs: $A(x_0, x_2)$, $A(x_2, x_3)$, $A(x_3, x_4)$ and $A(x_4, x_0)$. Here $A(x_p, x_q)$ denotes the arc joining $x_p, x_q$ which does not contain any other $x_j, j\in \{0,2,3,4\}$. With respect to this embedding into $C$, the point $x_1$ must lie on one of these arcs, and (i) holds precisely when $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$. Now, the assumption that $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ means that the diagonal $[x_0, x_2]$ crosses the diagonal $[x_1, x_4]$ which means that $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) by locating $x_1$ on a circle.

nodes.name: Arcs from the dihedral order
nodes.statement: Let $J\hookrightarrow C$ be an embedding into a circle defining the dihedral order. Since $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$, we have that $x_0, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are in the right dihedral order. In other words, their embedding into a circle $C$ is such that they subdivide $C$ into the following (unoriented) arcs: $A(x_0, x_2)$, $A(x_2, x_3)$, $A(x_3, x_4)$ and $A(x_4, x_0)$. Here $A(x_p, x_q)$ denotes the arc joining $x_p, x_q$ which does not contain any other $x_j, j\in \{0,2,3,4\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$ gives arcs between $x_0,x_2,x_3,x_4$.

nodes.name: Locate x_1
nodes.statement: With respect to this embedding into $C$, the point $x_1$ must lie on one of these arcs, and (i) holds precisely when $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: (i) holds iff $x_1\in A(x_0,x_2)$.

nodes.name: Use diagonal crossing
nodes.statement: Now, the assumption that $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ means that the diagonal $[x_0, x_2]$ crosses the diagonal $[x_1, x_4]$ which means that $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ forces $x_1\in A(x_0,x_2)$.

nodes.name: (iii) implies (i)
nodes.statement: The proof that (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is similar. In fact, the conditions $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$ and $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ already imply (i), the situation differing from (ii) by a cyclic rotation.
nodes.statement_short: Similar, up to cyclic rotation.

nodes.name: Lifts of torsors along abelian extensions
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a topological space and \[ 0\to A\longrightarrow\Gamma'\buildrel\pi\over\longrightarrow \Gamma\to 1 \] be an extension of sheaves of groups on $X$ with abelian kernel $A$. Let $P$ be a sheaf of $\Gamma$-torsors on $X$, with associated class $[P]\in H^1(X, \Gamma)$. In this situation, the $\Gamma$-action on $A$ by conjugation gives rise to the twisted form $A^P$, a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ locally isomorphic to $A$. Denote by $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ the category formed by sheaves $P'$ of $\Gamma'$-torsors on $X$ together with a $\pi$-equivariant map $\pi_{P'}: P'\to P$. Morphisms in $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ are isomorphisms of torsors commuting with the projection to $P$. In the described situation, we have:
nodes.statement_short: Set up an extension $A\to\Gamma'\to\Gamma$ and the category $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$.

nodes.name: Automorphisms of lifts
nodes.statement: [(i)] Each group $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_{\operatorname{Lift}(P)}(P')$ is identified with $H^0(X, A^P)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{Aut}=H^0(X,A^P)$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism classes of lifts
nodes.statement: [(ii)] The set of isomorphism classes of objects of $\operatorname{Lift}(P)$ is either empty or is a torsor over $H^1(X, A^P)$.
nodes.statement_short: Torsor over $H^1(X,A^P)$.

nodes.name: Obstruction
nodes.statement: [(iii)] If $A$ is central, then there is a natural coboundary map of pointed sets $\delta: H^1(X,\Gamma)\to H^2(X, A)$. In this case $\operatorname{Lift}(P)\neq\emptyset$ if and only if $\delta([P])=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Coboundary $\delta$ gives the obstruction to lifting.

nodes.name: Apply to G-structures
nodes.statement: Now, parts (a1-2) and (b1-2) follow by considering the extensions of sheaves on $S$ obtained from \eqref{eq:group-K} by passing to sheaves of $C^\infty$-sections. Part (b3) follows from Proposition \ref{prop:group-K}(b).
nodes.statement_short: Apply to sheaves from (3.1.1); (b3) from Proposition 3.1(b).

nodes.name: Kernel is Aut(F)
nodes.statement_short: Kernel is $\operatorname{Aut}(F)$, abelian by Proposition 3.4.

nodes.name: Image as stabilizer
nodes.statement: Further, $\phi\in\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$ lies in $\operatorname{Im}(\pi)$ if and only if the $\mathbb{G}$-structure $\phi^*F$ on $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$ is isomorphic to $F$. So $\operatorname{Im}(\pi)$ is the stabilizer of the action of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$ on the set of isomorphism classes of objects of $\mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))$.
nodes.statement_short: Image is the stabilizer of the isomorphism class of $F$.

nodes.name: Open and closed
nodes.statement: This set was described in Proposition \ref {prop:G-structures} (a2)(b2), in particular, it is discrete. So $\operatorname{Im}(\pi)$ is open and closed, and similarly for $\operatorname{Im}(\pi_{\operatorname{pure}})$.
nodes.statement_short: The set of classes is discrete, so the image is open and closed.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: (a) By definition, we have \[ G_{\operatorname{conf}} = \mathbb{G} \times_{GL(2,\mathbb{R})} O(2)_{{\operatorname{conf}}} \] where $O(2)_{{\operatorname{conf}}}={\operatorname{Conf}}(2)$. So given a $\mathbb{G}$-structure $F\to \operatorname{Fr}_S$ and an $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure $F^{O(2)}_{\operatorname{conf}} \to\operatorname{Fr}_S$, we obtain a $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structure by forming the fiber product \[ F_{\operatorname{conf}} \,\,=\,\, F\times_{\operatorname{Fr}_S} F^{O(2)}_{\operatorname{conf}} \] which is a principal $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-bundle. We leave the remaining details to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Fiber product of a $\mathbb{G}$-structure and a conformal structure.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: (b) Follows because $O(2)_{{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is a subgroup of $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.statement_short: $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\subset GL(2,\mathbb{R})$.

nodes.name: Decompose the quotient
nodes.statement: Using \eqref{eq:prod-str}, we have \begin{align*} \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) & = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \bigl( \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ)) \times O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\bigr)\\ & = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \biggl\backslash \hskip -.25cm \biggl\backslash \coprod_{ \{F\}\in \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))} O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\\ & = \coprod _{ \{F\}\in \operatorname{Diff}(S,M) \backslash \hskip -.1cm \backslash \mathbb{G}\operatorname{Str}(S-(M\cap S^\circ))} \biggl( \operatorname{Stab}(F) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\biggr). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split the quotient over orbits of $\mathbb{G}$-structures.

nodes.name: Stabilizers
nodes.statement: Note that at the bottom of last coproduct the quotient by $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$ is $\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$. At the same time, $\operatorname{Stab}(F)$ is the union of connected components of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$, in particular, $\operatorname{Stab}(F)_e = \operatorname{Diff}(S,M)_e$.
nodes.statement_short: Stabilizers are unions of components of $\operatorname{Diff}(S,M)$.

nodes.name: Identify with Teichmuller quotients
nodes.statement: Therefore the above coproduct can be identified with \[ \begin{gathered} \coprod_{ \{F\}\in\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \pi_0 (\operatorname{Stab}(F)) \biggl\backslash \hskip -.25cm \biggl\backslash \biggl( \operatorname{Stab}(F)_e \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)\biggr)\,\,= \\ =\,\, \coprod_{ \{F\} \in\mathcal{M}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)} \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S_F, M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) \end{gathered} \] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as quotients of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ by $\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S_F,M)$.

nodes.name: Conformal structures have no automorphisms
nodes.statement: In the last identification, we identified the topological groupoid $O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}\operatorname{Str}(S)$ with the topological space $\operatorname{Klein}(S)$ of its isomorphism classes. This is possible because all automorphism groups of objects in this groupoid are trivial by Proposition \ref{prop:prod-of-grpds}(b).
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 3.15(b).

nodes.name: Half-edge paths
nodes.statement: Let $h$ be a half-edge of $\Gamma$ incident to the vertex $v$ and with corresponding edge $e=\{h,h'\}$. We denote by $\gamma(|h|)$ the corresponding path in $S$ which runs from $\gamma(v)$ to the midpoint $m(e)= \gamma(e)$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce paths $\gamma(|h|)$ to edge midpoints.

nodes.name: Structures on objects
nodes.statement: A $\mathbb{G}$-structure on $S$ gives, via the homotopy equivalence $\mathbb{G}\to{ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$, a ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure on each circle $C(T_xS)$. Therefore, by Corollary \ref{cor:structured-circle-orders}, each finite subset of $C(T_xS)$ becomes, canonically, a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set. In particular, for each vertex $v \in V$, we have a canonical embedding of sets $H(v)\hookrightarrow C(T_{\gamma(v)} S)$ given by association to a half-edge $h$ the direction given by the germ of the path $\gamma(|h|)$ leaving $v$. By the above, this provides a canonical ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure on the set $H(v)$. Further, let $e$ be an edge of $\Gamma$ given by a pair of half-edges $h, h'$ as above. The two tangent directions to $|\Gamma|$ at $\gamma(m(e))$ correspond to the two half-edges $h$ and $h'$ of $e$. As before, the embedding $|\Gamma|\to S$ gives a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure on the 2-element set of these directions, i.e., on $\{h,h'\}$. This defines the values of the functor $\widetilde I_\Gamma: I(\Gamma)\to \mathcal{G}$ on objects.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 2.15 gives $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structures on $H(v)$ and $\{h,h'\}$.

nodes.name: Structured direction circles at v and e
nodes.statement_short: Introduce circles $C_v,C_e$ and arcs $A,B$.

nodes.name: Space Phi of homeomorphisms
nodes.statement: Similarly, let $J_e=A'\sqcup B'\subset C_e$ where $A'$ is a small closed arc around the image of $h$ in $C_e$ (denoted $a'$) and $B'$ is a small closed arc around the image of $h'$ in $C_e$ (denoted $b'$). Note that the orientation torsors of $C_v$ and $C_e$ are identified by parallel transport along $\gamma(|h|)$. We now consider the space $\Phi$ formed by all orientation preserving homeomorphisms \[ \phi: (C_v, J_v) \longrightarrow (C_e, J_e) \quad \text{s.t. } \phi(A)\subset A', \, \phi(B)\subset B'. \] These requirements define $\phi$ uniquely up to an isotopy (i.e., $\Phi$ is connected). Further, by Proposition \ref{prop:homeo-contr}, $\Phi$ is contractible. Consider now the unramified covering \[ \pi: { \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(C_v, C_e) \longrightarrow { \operatorname{Homeo}}(C_v, C_e). \] As $\Phi$ is contractible, $\pi^{-1}(\Phi)$ is a disjoint union of components homeomorphic to $\Phi$.
nodes.statement_short: The space $\Phi$ of marked homeomorphisms is contractible.

nodes.name: Canonical component
nodes.statement: We now show that the $\mathbb{G}$-structure on $S$ defines a canonical choice of a component $\widetilde\Phi\subset\pi^{-1}(\Phi)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:CG=DG}, $\widetilde\Phi$ will define a structure morphism $H(v)\to \{e,e'\}$ in $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: A canonical component $\widetilde\Phi$ gives the structure morphism by Theorem 2.13.

nodes.name: Parallel transport
nodes.statement: Choose a Riemannian metric on $S$ (a contractible choice). This reduces the structure group of $S$ from $\mathbb{G}$ to $G$. Let $T: C_v\to C_e$ be the Riemannian parallel transport along $\gamma(|h|)$. It lifts canonically to a morphism of ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structured circles. Denote this structured morphism by $\widetilde T$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Riemannian parallel transport $T$ and its structured lift $\widetilde T$.

nodes.name: Paths of homeomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\Pi$ be the space of paths $(T_s)_{s\in[0,1]}$ in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(C_v, C_e)$ starting at $T$ and ending somewhere in $\Phi$. Any path $(T_s)\in\Pi$ defines a lift $\widetilde\Phi$ by transporting $\widetilde T$ along this path. Clearly, this $\widetilde \Phi$ depends only on the image of $(T_s)$ in $\pi_0(\Pi)$. Note that $\pi_0(\Pi)$ is a torsor over $\mathbb{Z} = \pi_1 \,{ \operatorname{Homeo}}^+(C_v, C_e)$.
nodes.statement_short: Paths from $T$ into $\Phi$; $\pi_0(\Pi)$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor.

nodes.name: Distinguished component
nodes.statement: Note that $T$ sends the midpoint $b\in B$ (i.e, the image of $h$ in $C_v$) into the midpoint $b'\in B'$ (i.e., the image of $h'$ in $C_e$). Therefore we have a distinguished component $\Pi_0$ of $\Pi$ containing paths $(T_s)$ such that $T_s(B)$ meets $B'$ for all $s$. The transport of $\widetilde T$ along any path from $\Pi_0$ gives the component $\widetilde\Phi$. This concludes the argument.
nodes.statement_short: Paths keeping $T_s(B)$ meeting $B'$ select $\widetilde\Phi$.

nodes.name: Normalize the interval
nodes.statement: Given an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured interval as in \eqref{eq:interval}, note that $\varphi_e$ and $\varphi_f$ are isomorphisms in ${\mathcal G}$. Using $\varphi_e$ to identify $H(v)$ with $[1]$, we obtain that the augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-strutured interval is isomorphic to \[ [1] \overset{\operatorname{id}}{\longleftarrow} [1] \overset{g}{\longrightarrow} [1] \] where $g$ is an automorphism of $[1]$ which induces the identity on the underlying set $\{0,1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $H(v)$ with $[1]$ via $\varphi_e$.

nodes.name: Identify with G_1^0
nodes.statement: Therefore, we have $g \in \mathfrak{G}_1^0$ where $\mathfrak{G}_1^0$ denotes the kernel of the map $\lambda: \mathfrak{G}_1 \to S_2$ from Proposition \ref{prop:forget}. It is immediate to verify that this identitication is compatible with the group law on $\mathfrak{G}_1^0$.
nodes.statement_short: $g$ lies in the kernel of $\lambda$; compatible with group law.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: Part (1) is clear.
nodes.statement_short: Operad axioms are clear.

nodes.name: Contract to corollas
nodes.statement: We show (2). Given an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured tree $\Gamma$ in $\operatorname{Tr}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(n)$ with augmented incidence diagram $I(\Gamma) \to {\mathcal G}$, we first argue that we can contract all internal edges to obtain a corolla.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce trees to corollas by contracting internal edges.

nodes.name: Edge collapse via limits
nodes.statement: To this end, we note that, given an internal edge $\{e,e'\}$ incident to vertices $v$ and $v'$, the corresponding diagram \[ H(v) \longrightarrow \{e,e'\} \longleftarrow H(v') \] has a limit in ${\mathcal G}$ whose underlying set is given by $(H(v)\setminus \{e\}) \cup (H(v') \setminus \{e'\})$. This holds for all planar crossed simplicial groups and can be verified using the topological model of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ from \S \ref{sec:topmodel}. We can use the cone diagram of this limit in ${\mathcal G}$ to produce a morphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma \to \Gamma'$ which collapses the edge $\{e,e'\}$. After collapsing all internal edges of $\Gamma$, we obtain an augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla $\Gamma_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Limits in $\mathcal{G}$ collapse internal edges.

nodes.name: Normalize corolla
nodes.statement: Using the labels we can identify the set $H(v)$ of halfedges incident to the single vertex of $\Gamma_0$ with $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. We can find an isomorphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $f: (\{0,1,\dots,n\}, {\mathcal O}) \cong [n]$ and since, for planar crossed simplicial groups, $\mathfrak{G}_n$ acts (simply) transitively on $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([0],[n])$ we may assume that $f$ maps $0$ to $0$. Therefore, after permuting the labels $1,2, \dots, n$, we may assume that $H(v) = [n]$. Every morphism $[n] \to [1]$ such that $\varphi^{-1}(0) = \{0\}$ (corresponding to the outgoing halfedge labeled $0$) can be written as a composite $\varphi g$ where $\varphi: [n] \to [1]$ is the morphism in $\Delta$ which maps $0$ to $0$ and all remaining elements to $1$, and $g \in \operatorname{Stab}(0) \subset \mathfrak{G}_n$. Therefore, we can assume that the augmentation $H(v) = [n] \to [1]$ of the single outgoing halfedge $0$ is given by $\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the outgoing augmentation using transitivity of $\mathfrak{G}_n$.

nodes.name: Torsor of labelled corollas
nodes.statement: For every $1 \le i \le n$, the subset of $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}([n],[1])$ given by those morphisms such that $\varphi^{-1}(1) = \{i\}$ forms a torsor under the action of $\mathfrak{G}_1^0 \cong \mathfrak{G}_0$. Note that this action of $\mathfrak{G}_0$ is precisely the operadic action of the monoid $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ on the incoming halfedges. Therefore, the collection of isomorphism classes of labelled augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corollas forms a torsor under the action of \[ \underbrace{P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1) \times P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1) \times \dots \times P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)}_n \times S_{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Labelled corollas form a torsor under $P(1)^n\times S_n$.

nodes.name: Trivialize via duality
nodes.statement: We will now trivialize this torsor, for every $n$, by choosing a specific ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla in such a way that these chosen $n$-corollas are closed under operadic composition (for $n>1$). To this end, choose a duality functor $D: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ and consider the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ [1] \ar[drr]_{\{0,1\}}& [1] \ar[dr]^{\{1,2\}} & \dots & [1] \ar[dl]^{\{n-1,n\}}\\ & & [n] & \\ & & [1]\ar[u]^{\{0,n\}} & } \] in $\Delta \subset {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ and apply $D$ to obtain the incidence diagram of a labeled augmented ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured $n$-corolla which we define to be our chosen trivialization. It is easy to verify that, due to the functoriality of $D$, the collection of corollas thus obtained is closed under operadic composition.
nodes.statement_short: Choose corollas via a duality functor, closed under composition.

nodes.name: Twisted associative algebras
nodes.statement: This exhibits a copy of the associative operad $\operatorname{Ass}$ in $P$ such that every element of $P$ can be uniquely expressed as an element of $\operatorname{Ass}$ precomposed with elements of the monoid $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ acting on the incoming halfedges. An explicit computation of the action of $P_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}}(1)$ on the outgoing halfedges of $\operatorname{Ass}$ in terms of the actions on the incoming halfedges implies the claim that $P$ parametrizes algebras with twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action.
nodes.statement_short: $P$ is $\operatorname{Ass}$ twisted by $P(1)=\mathfrak{G}_0$.

nodes.name: (a) Oriented case
nodes.statement: \underbar{(a) Oriented case } $G=SO(2)$. In this case, the statement (that the usual moduli space of stable marked {\em Riemann surfaces} has an orbicell decomposition labelled by ribbon graphs) is well known, see, e.g., \cite{arbarello, penner:book} and references therein. We indicate here the main steps which we later analyze to deduce the general case. First, each component of $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is a quotient groupoid \[ \mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Mod}^+(S,M)\bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M). \] Second, $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ has a $\operatorname{Mod}^+(S,M)$-invariant regular cell decomposition (triangulation) constructed by Harer \cite{harer} and described in Appendix \ref {subsub:harer}. Denote this cell decomposition by ${\mathcal Y}$. The simplices of ${\mathcal Y}$ correspond to tesselations of $(S,M)$ or, dually, to isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$. Inclusions of simplices correspond to coarsenings of tesselations or, dually, to contractions of spanning graphs. Any spanning graph for $(S,M)$ carries an induced ribbon structure. Therefore, orbicells in the quotient orbicell decomposition, which we denote $\mathcal{X}_{S,M}$, form a full subcategory in $\Lambda-\operatorname{Graph}$ with objects those graphs that appear as spanning graphs for $(S,M)$. Finally, each ribbon graph $\Gamma$ gives rise to an oriented marked surface $(S,M)$ obtained by ``thickening" $\Gamma$, so that $\Gamma$ becomes a spanning graph for $(S,M)$, see, e.g., \cite{HSS-triangulated} \S 3.3.4. This shows that for $\mathcal{X}=\coprod_{(S,M)} \mathcal{X}_{S,M}$, we have ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq {\Lambda}-\operatorname{Graph}$. Note that Costello \cite{costello-dual} introduced another topological groupoid $\mathcal{N}$ with an orbicell decomposition labelled by ${\Lambda}-\operatorname{Graph}$ which is homotopy equivalent, but not homeomorphic to $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Harer's triangulation of $\operatorname{Teich}^+$ and ribbon graphs.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Quotient description
nodes.statement: First, each component of $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ is a quotient groupoid \[ \mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Mod}^+(S,M)\bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M). \]
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M)=\operatorname{Mod}^+\backslash\backslash\operatorname{Teich}^+$.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Harer triangulation
nodes.statement: Second, $\operatorname{Teich}^+(S,M)$ has a $\operatorname{Mod}^+(S,M)$-invariant regular cell decomposition (triangulation) constructed by Harer \cite{harer} and described in Appendix \ref {subsub:harer}. Denote this cell decomposition by ${\mathcal Y}$. The simplices of ${\mathcal Y}$ correspond to tesselations of $(S,M)$ or, dually, to isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$. Inclusions of simplices correspond to coarsenings of tesselations or, dually, to contractions of spanning graphs. Any spanning graph for $(S,M)$ carries an induced ribbon structure. Therefore, orbicells in the quotient orbicell decomposition, which we denote $\mathcal{X}_{S,M}$, form a full subcategory in $\Lambda-\operatorname{Graph}$ with objects those graphs that appear as spanning graphs for $(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Simplices correspond to spanning graphs, which are ribbon graphs.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Thickening
nodes.statement: Finally, each ribbon graph $\Gamma$ gives rise to an oriented marked surface $(S,M)$ obtained by ``thickening" $\Gamma$, so that $\Gamma$ becomes a spanning graph for $(S,M)$, see, e.g., \cite{HSS-triangulated} \S 3.3.4. This shows that for $\mathcal{X}=\coprod_{(S,M)} \mathcal{X}_{S,M}$, we have ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq {\Lambda}-\operatorname{Graph}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every ribbon graph is spanning for its thickening.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Costello's dual model
nodes.statement: Note that Costello \cite{costello-dual} introduced another topological groupoid $\mathcal{N}$ with an orbicell decomposition labelled by ${\Lambda}-\operatorname{Graph}$ which is homotopy equivalent, but not homeomorphic to $\mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Comparison with Costello's groupoid.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: (b) Unoriented case
nodes.statement: \underbar{(b) Unoriented case} $G=O(2)$. It is treated similarly to the oriented case, using the identification \[ \mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}(S,M) \,\,=\,\,\operatorname{Mod}(S,M) \bigl\backslash \hskip -.1cm \bigl\backslash \operatorname{Teich}(S,M) \] and the triangulation ${\mathcal Y}$ of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ described in \S \ref{subsub:harer}. As before, the simplices of ${\mathcal Y}$ correspond to triangulations of $(S,M)$ and give M\"obius graphs as $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-orbits. Further, any M\"obius graph $\Gamma$ can be ``thickened" producing an unoriented surface $(S,M)$ in which it is spanning. So, for the resulting quotient orbicell decomposition $\mathcal{X}$ of $\mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ we have ${\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X})\simeq {\Xi}-\operatorname{Graph}$. Note that an analog of Costello's approach \cite{costello-dual} for Klein surfaces was developed by Braun \cite{braun}.
nodes.statement_short: Same with $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ and Möbius graphs.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: (c) General case
nodes.statement_short: Pull back along the forgetful covering and compare.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Preimage decomposition
nodes.statement: Depending on whether $G$ preserves orientation or not, we consider one of the two projections \[ \pi: \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}^{SO(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}, \quad \pi: \mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}} \] obtained by forgetting the extra structure. In each case, the projection $\pi$ is an unramified covering of orbifolds, so the preimage of any orbicell in the target is a disjoint union of orbicells in the source. We thus obtain an orbicell decomposition of $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ which we now analyze. We sketch the case when $G$ does not preserve the orientation, the other case being similar but easier.
nodes.statement_short: The forgetful projection is an unramified covering of orbifolds.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Commutative square of categories
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{X}$ the orbicell decomposition of $\mathcal{M}^{O(2)_{\operatorname{conf}}}$ and by $\mathcal{X}^G$ the preimage decomposition of $\mathcal{M}^{G_{\operatorname{conf}}}$. Since any $G_{\operatorname{conf}}$-structured marked surface is $\mathbb{G}$-structured, any tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of the surface makes the dual graph of $\mathcal{P}$ into a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph. We obtain therefore a commutative diagram of categories \[ \xymatrix{ {\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X}^G) \ar[d]_{q_G} \ar[r]^{\pi} & {\operatorname{Cell}}(\mathcal{X}) \ar[d]^q \\ {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \ar[r]_\varpi & {\Xi}-\operatorname{Graph} } \] where $q$ is an equivalence by the case (b) above.
nodes.statement_short: Square relating $\operatorname{Cell}(\mathcal{X}^G)$ and graph categories.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: q_G is an equivalence
nodes.statement_short: Show $q_G$ is an equivalence.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Fibers are torsors
nodes.statement_short: Fibers on both sides are torsors for relative automorphism groups.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Reduce to Lemma 4.26
nodes.statement: Since we already know that the map $q$ is fully faithful, to show that $q^G$ is fully faithful, it therefore suffices to show that the induced map \[ \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(\sigma'/\pi(\sigma')) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(q^G(\sigma')/q^G(\pi(\sigma'))) \] is bijective. Showing this statement and the essential surjectivity of $q^G$ amounts to showing that $q^G$ induces an equivalence of all strict fiber categories of $\pi$ and $\varpi$. This is shown in the following lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to equivalence of fiber categories, the lemma.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Essential surjectivity
nodes.statement: We first show that $q_\Gamma$ is essentially surjective. Let $F_\Gamma$ be a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure on $\Gamma$. By Theorem \ref{thm:CG=DG}, $F_\Gamma$ can be seen as a datum, for each $x\in\Gamma\subset S'$, of a ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure on the circle of directions $C_x(S)$. Moreover, these structures are compatible as $x$ moves in $\Gamma$, thus providing a ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure on $C(T_S)|_\Gamma$, the restriction to $\Gamma$ of the circle bundle $C(T_S)$. Since $\Gamma$ is homotopy equivalent to $S-M$ and hence to $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$, we get a unique, up to isomorphism, ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure on $C(T_{S-(M\cap S^\circ)})$. Finally, since $\mathbb{G}\to{ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$ is a homotopy equivalence, we obtain from this a $\mathbb{G}$-structure on $S-(M\cap S^\circ)$. Thus $q_\Gamma$ is essentially surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the structured circle bundle from $\Gamma$ to the surface.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Full faithfulness
nodes.statement_short: Compare automorphism sheaves with $\underline K^{\operatorname{or}}$.
nodes.section: 4.4.2 Decompositions of the structured moduli spaces

nodes.name: Data of a morphism
nodes.statement: A morphism $\varphi$ between ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ consists of a functor $\varphi: I(\Gamma) \to I(\Gamma')$ of incidence categories together with a natural transformation $\eta: \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \circ \varphi \to \widetilde{I}_\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: A functor of incidence categories with a natural transformation.

nodes.name: Induced map of limits
nodes.statement: We obtain a canonical sequence of morphisms \[ \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \longrightarrow \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \varphi \overset{\eta}{\longrightarrow} \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma} \] whose composite defines the desired morphism ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma'} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$. Here the first morphism is the natural morphism $\lim F \to \lim F \varphi$ which exists for any functor $F: I(\Gamma') \to \mathbf{C}$ provided that both limits exist. It is straightforward to verify the functoriality of this association.
nodes.statement_short: Compose induced maps of limits.

nodes.name: RX on structured graphs
nodes.statement: Consider the functor \[ {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}, \; \Gamma \mapsto RX(\Gamma). \] Due to the $2$-Segal property of $X$, it maps weak equivalences of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs to weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: $RX$ sends weak equivalences to weak equivalences by 2-Segality.

nodes.name: Classifying spaces
nodes.statement: We can pass to classifying spaces to obtain a map of topological spaces. \[ |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}| \] where $W_{\mathbf{C}}$ denotes the category of weak equivalences in $\mathbf{C}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:g-graph}, we have \[ |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \simeq \coprod_{(S,M)} B\, \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) \] so that we obtain, for every stable $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface $(S,M)$, a map \[ \rho: B\, \operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M) \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use Theorem 4.12 to get $\rho:B\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)\to|W_\mathbf{C}|$.

nodes.name: Coherent action
nodes.statement: The topological space $|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$ is a model for the maximal $\infty$-groupoid in the simplicial localization of $\mathbf{C}$ with respect to $W$ (cf. \cite{dwyer-kan}). Therefore, the map $\rho$ realizes a coherent action of the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^\mathbb{G}(S,M)$ on $\rho(*) \cong X(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: $|W_\mathbf{C}|$ models the maximal $\infty$-groupoid.

nodes.name: Reduce to polygon gluing
nodes.statement: To verify the $2$-Segal property, we have to show that, for any subdivision of the $n+1$-gon $P_n$ into two polygons $P_m$ with vertices $\{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}$ and $P_l$ with vertices $\{i,i+1,\dots, j\}$, the corresponding functor \[ f: \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}) \coprod_{\Pi_1(D, \{i,j\})} \Pi_1(D, \{i,i+1,\dots, j\}) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\}) \] is an isomorphism of groupoids.
nodes.statement_short: Need $f$ to be an isomorphism for every polygon subdivision.

nodes.name: Polygon description
nodes.statement: Up to isomorphism of groupoids we can alternatively describe $f$ as the natural functor \[ f': \Pi_1(P_m) \coprod_{\Pi_1(P_1)} \Pi_1(P_l) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(P_n) \] induced from expressing $P_n$ as the union of $P_m$ and $P_l$ with intersection $P_m \cap P_l = P_1$. Here, all fundamental groupoids are taken with respect to the vertices of the respective polygon.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $f$ via fundamental groupoids of polygons.

nodes.name: Van Kampen
nodes.statement: The fact that $f'$ is an isomorphism of groupoids is an easy instance of van Kampen's theorem (see, e.g., \cite[6.7.2]{brown}).
nodes.statement_short: Van Kampen's theorem.

nodes.name: Compute F(S,M)
nodes.statement: Similarly, to compute $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$, note that we can pass to the dual of a spanning graph in $S \setminus M$ to express $(S,M)$ as a union of polygons. Interpreting formula \eqref{eq:statesum} in these terms, another application of van Kampen's theorem shows that $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ is the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ computed as a colimit parametrized by the above polygonal subdivision of $(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Dual polygonal decomposition and van Kampen give $\Pi_1(S,M)$.

nodes.name: Covering by closed simplices
nodes.statement: We consider the covering $\mathcal{U}$ of $|A|-|A'|$ by closed subsets $\Delta^I_0 = \Delta^I \cap (|A|-|A'|)$ for $I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'$.
nodes.statement_short: Cover by $\Delta^I_0$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Monotone nerve
nodes.statement: This covering is saturated, and $(A,A')^\vee=\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U}$.
nodes.statement_short: $(A,A')^\vee=\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U}$.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Nerve theorem
nodes.statement: As each $\Delta^I_0$ is contractible, our statement follows from Proposition \ref{prop:nerve-classical}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition A.6.
nodes.section: A.2 The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Extend Harer
nodes.statement: The construction and the argument of \cite{harer} extend to the general case as follows.
nodes.statement_short: Harer's construction extends.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Construct Psi
nodes.statement: A point $p\in |A|-|A_\infty|$ lies, by definition, strictly inside a simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ for some tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ and thus is represented by the collection of its barycentric coordinates \[ (p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}, \,\, p_\gamma > 0,\,\, \sum p_\gamma = 1, \] one for each arc $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}$. Consider a polygon $(S'_i, M'_i)$ of $\mathcal{P}$. To each edge $e$ of $S'_i$ we associate the ``length" $p_e:=p_\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is the arc of $\mathcal{P}$ that gave rise to $e$. Let $l_e=\sum_{e\subset\partial S'_i} p_e$ be the total ``length" of $\partial S'_i$. Let $S''_i$ be a disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with center $0$ and circumference $l_e$. We can map $M'_i$ bijectively to a subset $M''_i\subset \partial S''_i$ so that the distances (on $\partial S''_i$) between neighboring elements of $M''_i$ match the corresponding numbers $p_e$ for the edges of $S'_i$. In this way we get a stable marked Klein surface $(S''_i, M''_i)$. We now glue the $(S''_i, M''_i)$ together in the same fashion as the $(S'_i, M'_i)$ are glued together to form $(S, M)$. For this, we use the identifications of the boundary arcs of different $S''_i$ which are affine linear in the standard angle (or arc length) coordinates on the circles $\partial S''_i$. In this way we get a Klein surface $(S'', M'')$, identified with $(S,M)$ by a diffeomorphism unique up to isotopy. In other words, we get a point of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$. This defines the map $\Psi_{S,M}$. Its $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-equivariance is clear.
nodes.statement_short: Glue disks with boundary lengths given by barycentric coordinates.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Oriented case
nodes.statement: The fact that $\Psi_{S,M}$ is a homeomorphism, was proved in \cite{harer} in the oriented case.
nodes.statement_short: Harer.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Reduce to fixed points
nodes.statement: Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, and let $\varpi: (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)\to (S,M)$ be its orientation cover, with the deck involution $\tau$ preserving $\widetilde M$. By equivariance, the homeomorphism \[ \Psi_{\widetilde S, \widetilde M}: \,\, |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)| \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich} (\widetilde S, \widetilde M) \] sends the involution $\tau_A: |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\to |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|$ induced by $\tau$, to $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. Because of Proposition \ref{thm:klein-teich}(b2), we are reduced to the following.
nodes.statement_short: Use the orientation cover and Theorem 3.19(b2).
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Lemma A.10 and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{lem} We have \[ \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \,\,=\,\, |A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|. \] \end{lem} \noindent {\sl Proof of the lemma:} A point $p\in |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|^{\tau_A}$ lies in a $\tau$-invariant simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ corresponding to a $\tau$-invariant sub-tesselation $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ of $(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}$. We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$ does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering). So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation. Further, suppose that $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation, Then any polygon $(\widetilde S'_i, \widetilde M'_i)$ of $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation. We conclude that \[ p\,\,\in \,\, \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \] must lie in a simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ where $\widetilde\mathcal{P}=\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{P})$ is the preimage of a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of $(S,M)$ and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates $(p_{\widetilde\gamma})_{{\widetilde\gamma}\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ which is $\tau$-invariant. Such collections of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ in $|A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|$. This proves the lemma and Theorem \ref{thm:harer-triang}.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points of $\tau_A$.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Invariant sub-tessellation
nodes.statement: A point $p\in |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|^{\tau_A}$ lies in a $\tau$-invariant simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ corresponding to a $\tau$-invariant sub-tesselation $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ of $(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: $p$ lies in a $\tau$-invariant simplex; project arcs.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Projection is a sub-tessellation
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$ does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering). So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tessellation.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: No self-intersection
nodes.statement: Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$ does not intersect itself.
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness of $\widetilde\gamma$ and $\tau\widetilde\gamma$.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Distinct arcs
nodes.statement: Further, a homotopy between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering). So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation.
nodes.statement_short: Unramified covering lifts homotopies.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Tessellations project
nodes.statement: Further, suppose that $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation, Then any polygon $(\widetilde S'_i, \widetilde M'_i)$ of $\widetilde\mathcal{P}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation.
nodes.statement_short: Polygons cover polygons.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Coordinates match
nodes.statement: We conclude that \[ p\,\,\in \,\, \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \] must lie in a simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ where $\widetilde\mathcal{P}=\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{P})$ is the preimage of a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of $(S,M)$ and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates $(p_{\widetilde\gamma})_{{\widetilde\gamma}\in\widetilde\mathcal{P}}$ which is $\tau$-invariant. Such collections of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the simplex $\Delta^\mathcal{P}$ in $|A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|$. This proves the lemma and Theorem \ref{thm:harer-triang}.
nodes.statement_short: Invariant barycentric coordinates correspond to points of $|A(S,M)|$.
nodes.section: A.3 Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
